#2752. NFL playoff picture: How things stand ahead of Bears-Seahawks

With the calendar now flipped to November, the NFL is entering the push to the playoffs.

So it is the perfect time to start looking at how the playoff picture is shaping up.

Week 8 of the NFL season delivered some surprises, and as such some team are currently on the outside looking in when it comes to the postseason. And with a big game on tap for Monday Night Football, the playoff picture might look even more different come Tuesday morning.

Here is how the AFC standings look, with all AFC teams now finished for Week 8.

1. Buffalo Bills (6-1)2. Denver Broncos (6-2)3. Pittsburgh Steelers (6-2)4. Jacksonville Jaguars (5-2)5. Kansas City Chiefs (5-2)6. Cincinnati Bengals (5-2)7. New England Patriots (5-3)

8. Cleveland Browns (5-3)9. Las Vegas Raiders (4-4)10. Baltimore Ravens (4-4)11. Houston Texans (2-5)12. New York Jets (2-6)13. Indianapolis Colts (2-6)14. Miami Dolphins (1-6)15. Tennessee Titans (1-7)16. Los Angeles Chargers (0-7)

We can start at the bottom and work up, as things are rather self-explanatory until we reach the Jets and the Colts. Those two teams have matching records, but right now the Jets are ahead of the Colts as New York has a 2-3 record in conference play, while Indianaplis is just 1-5 in AFC games.

Either way the Jets are winners, as they control the Colts' first-round pick thanks to the Sauce Gardner trade.

The Raiders and the Ravens have matching 4-4 records, but Las Vegas has a 3-3 conference record, while Baltimore is just 2-3 in AFC games so far this year.

The Patriots and the Browns have matching 5-3 records, but New England's 5-1 AFC record has them in the No. 7 spot right now, while Cleveland's 3-3 record in conference games has them on the outside looking in. Then the Broncos, who moved into first place in the AFC West with Sunday's win over Kansas City, take the No. 2 spot from the Steelers. While both teams are 6-2, Denver is 3-1 in the AFC, while Pittsburgh is 3-2.

Here are the hypothetical playoff matchups, if the AFC playoffs started today:

1. San Francisco 49ers (6-1)2. Minnesota Vikings (6-1)3. New York Giants (4-2-1)4. Carolina Panthers (3-4)5. Detroit Lions (5-2)6. Chicago Bears (5-2)7. Green Bay Packers (5-3)

8. Seattle Seahawks (4-3)9. Los Angeles Rams (4-4)10. Tampa Bay Buccaneers (3-5)11. Atlanta Falcons (3-5)12. Arizona Cardinals (3-5)13. Dallas Cowboys (3-5)14. Washington Commanders (2-4-1)15. New Orleans Saints (2-5)16. Philadelphia Eagles (2-6)

Let's start with the cluster of four 3-5 teams.

Under the NFL tiebreaking procedures, first you apply division tiebreakers to eliminate all but the highest-ranked team in each division. The Buccaneers beat the Falcons, so they have the tiebreaker, so that brings the process down to Tampa Bay, Arizona, and Dallas for the next step. Then both Tampa Bay and now Arizona have wins over the Cowboys, so that leaves the Buccaneers and the Cardinals.

Tampa Bay gets the nod right now thanks to a 3-2 record in the NFC, compared to a 2-4 conference record for the Cardinals.

Atlanta slots into the No. 11 spot in a three-way fight with Arizona and Dallas. The Falcons' 3-3 NFC record is better than both Arizona (2-4) and Dallas (2-4).

Arizona slots in at No. 12 thanks to Sunday's win over the Cowboys, who then slide into the No. 13 spot.

Things are a bit more straightforward among the seven teams currently in the playoffs. San Francisco takes the No. 1 spot over Minnesota thanks to a better Strength of Victory (.456 for San Francisco vs. .400 for Minnesota), because both teams have a 4-1 record in conference play, and they have not played enough common opponents as of yet.

The Lions hold the No. 5 spot over Chicago thanks to a better record in division games (2-0 for Detroit, 0-2 for Chicago).

Here are the hypothetical NFC playoff matchups if the playoffs started today:

Monday night's game between Chicago and Seattle is ripe with playoff implications, even this early in the season.

Not only could it set up a potential tiebreaker advantage for the winning team, but if the Bears were to win, it would bump them up to No. 5 in the NFC standings. A loss would drop Chicago into a three-way tie with the Packers and the Seahawks. Then, working through the tiebreakers, the Bears would drop out of the head-to-head with the Packers (as Chicago lost to Green Bay), and the Packers would slot in at No. 6 thanks to a better conference record (4-3 for Green Bay vs. 2-2 for Seattle. But the Seahawks would now be the No. 7 team, thanks to a win over Chicago, and the Bears would drop to No. 8.

But a Bears win would drop Seattle to 4-4, and they would drop behind the Rams to No. 9, thanks to a 1-3 record in NFC games (versus a 2-2 record for the Rams).

#2748. The Vikings should explore a trade for Daniel Jones

At a time when the Vikings are believed to be talking to the Colts about a potential trade for running back Jonathan Taylor, they should adjust their focal point, just a bit.

The Vikings should be talking to the Colts about a potential trade for quarterback Daniel Jones.

When the thought first popped into my somewhat relaxed brain on Sunday, I was mostly kidding. After reflecting on Sunday’s 19-15 loss to the Lions — and revisiting the rare displays of frustration from receiver Justin Jefferson late in the game and, even more significantly, from coach Kevin O’Connell when talking to quarterback Kyler Murray after an ugly interception late in the first half — it’s not a joke.

They should immediately pivot from Taylor to Jones.

The Vikings had Jones in the building two years ago, after he was released by the Giants. They wanted to keep him for 2025, more (by all appearances) than they wanted to keep Sam Darnold. (Indeed, there were whispers of a potential benching of Darnold for Jones in the 2024 postseason.)

Now that the Colts are in full-blown pre-rebuild mode, trading Jones should be part of the effort to clear the decks (and stockpile picks) for the next G.M. And while the Colts have a window to avoid more than $10 million of Jones’s $38 million compensation package for 2027 via a trade in the early days of the new league year in March, they could get more now from a contender that envisions Jones as an immediate upgrade.

Jones obviously won’t be the long-term answer in Indianapolis. And he would undoubtedly welcome the chance to move on from a team that prematurely threw in the towel last week by trading guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.

In Minnesota, Jones would be an immediate upgrade over Kyler Murray. The difference between Jones vs. Murray could be more significant than the difference between Jonathan Taylor and Aaron Jones/Jordan Mason. Which, if accurate, would result in a bigger overall bump to the offense.

The Vikings have a championship-caliber defense, thanks in large part to the work of defensive coordinator Brian Flores. The grind-it-out-and-get-a-win formula had been working — until it didn’t.

Here’s the inescapable reality. When they win with quarterback play that is inconsistent and, in turn, frustrating to people like Jefferson and O’Connell, it’s easy to overlook the flaws and keep pushing forward. When they lose, the frustrations of that moment become compounded by the lingering frustrations regarding plays and points left on the field in the wins that were salvaged by the defense.

Whether it’s Jones or someone else (including a possible pivot to Carson Wentz), O’Connell and G.M. Nolan Teasley need to conduct a frank, candid, and objective assessment of the quarterback play under Murray. The fact that they picked Murray over J.J. McCarthy shouldn’t be a factor. That’s the kind of pride/ego consideration that keeps dysfunctional teams dysfunctional by doubling down on a mistake instead of admitting it and moving on.

The Vikings need to realize that: (1) the defense is great; (2) the running game is good enough; and (3) the passing game is too spotty to be expected to make a big play in a big spot.

Consider the decision that O’Connell made with 3:01 to play on Sunday, when the Vikings faced fourth and five from their own 33. Down four points after the Detroit running game had hot-knife-through-buttered their way to the go-ahead touchdown, why give the ball back to the Lions and let them close out the game by continuing to lean on Jahmyr Gibbs?

In that moment, O’Connell thought the chances of winning were enhanced by punting — not by asking the offense to gain five yards in a gotta-have-it situation.

While the choice showed unwarranted confidence in the defense, it showed NO confidence in the quarterback.

Frankly, that one specific decision from O’Connell leads naturally to the next, more consequential decision that the organization must make. If O’Connell doesn’t trust the offense under Murray to gain five yards with the game on the line, the Vikings should no longer entrust the offense to Murray.

It’s that simple. And, if the Vikings hope to avoid an outcome to the season that will result in an every-other-year playoff appearance and another one-and-done postseason, they’ll make the decision that someone other than Murray should be playing quarterback.

At a time when politics have become a major national focal point, this would be a so-called 80-20 issue among Vikings fans. They’ve seen the “just good enough is just good enough” movie for decades. With the defense the Vikings currently have, the offense needs more. If they’re serious about having a snowball’s chance in San Diego to get back to the Super Bowl for the first time in 50 years, they’ll send Kyler to Belize and make a play for Jones.

Or someone else. See if the Raiders are willing to part with Kirk Cousins (they shouldn’t be, but why not make the call?) Call the Chargers about Justin Herbert. Scour every depth chart and start doing the due diligence.

When Cousins suffered a season-ending torn Achilles tendon just before the trade deadline in 2023, the Vikings mobilized instantly to find a replacement. Based on the full body of work from Murray to date in 2026, they should be doing the same thing now — if they want to parlay their 6-0 start into the best possible finish.

#2746. Rockets Jabari Smith Jr. has found his best self

No Houston Rockets fan has experienced a rebuild quite like this one.

Yes, there have been rebuilds. Some of you are old enough to remember the Rockets tanking for Hakeem Olajuwon even though they already had Ralph Sampson. That's probably the closest analog, but it's still not a top-down, from-scratch rebuild like the one we've been watching.

When the Olajuwon era was dying, and the Rockets landed Steve Francis, they got quickly off to the races. There was no more vying for high lottery picks. They pivoted to Yao Ming mid-era when their pick leaped. They were a plucky, competitive bunch until they stumbled into James Harden, and now we're here. The point?

We are not used to evaluating young players over here.

There is an underlying assumption that after four seasons, we "know who a player is". As far as assumptions go, this one isn't too far off base. Rare is the NBA player who stagnates in his fourth season, only to make "the leap".

It seems that Jabari Smith Jr. does not care for our assumptions.

Last year, Smith Jr. averaged 15.9 points per game while shooting 45.0% from the field and 36.8% from deep.

It was his best season, but only by a fairly narrow margin. OK, we (with some exceptions, I see you, Darren, shout out Big O) collectively thought. This is who he is.

It wasn't so bad! Smith Jr. was one of the best shooters in the NBA who could reasonably play any minutes at the 5. That's something. He had real defensive utility, even if he wasn't elite. Really, this was the floor version of Bari that was advertised during the draft process. Limited on-ball ability, defensively versatile 6'11" floor spacer. It wasn't sexy, but we were willing to take it.

But this year's version of Smith Jr. is downright sultry.

He's averaging 19.0 points per game while shooting 48.9% from the field and 44.7% from three-point range. This is closer to the ceiling version of Smith Jr.:

Smith Jr.'s shot profile has barely changed. In 2026-27, 51.1% of his field goals are coming from beyond the arc, compared to 50.1% last year. The rest of his attempts are spread fairly evenly from the deep two range to the paint, just as they were last season.

On paper, virtually all the improvement is coming from his three-point efficiency boost. So, that's a valid concern. Smith Jr. is unlikely to finish the season shooting 44.7% from deep.

It's worth noting that the data says Smith Jr. is mostly getting better shots this season. NBA.com classifies 25.7% of his field goals as wide open, compared to 18.5% in 2025-26.

The story underneath the story here is that it looks like Ime Udoka thought about offense this summer (I know, right?). He may have intentionally instilled defense and hustle principles for two seasons before expanding his playbook, but that's another article.

Back to Smith Jr.: He looks much more confident with the ball. He's attacking closeouts and getting to his spots. He is simply a better basketball player.

There have always been questions about Smith Jr., but none have ever pertained to his work ethic. He's always had the want. He's mostly made marginal improvements in every year of his career, and we're simply seeing the widest margin this season.

So yes, his three-point shooting is likely to regress. It's also pretty likely that this will be the best shooting (and, vicariously, overall) season of Smith Jr.'s career.

#2745. Cowboys had never blown a 14-point, fourth-quarter lead at home before Sunday

A third-party contractor yelled “embarrassing” to Dak Prescott as he walked back to the Cowboys’ locker room after a 24-16 loss to the Bucs in Week 5. The Cowboys’ 33-30 overtime loss to the Cardinals on Sunday was arguably worse.

Before Sunday, the Cowboys were 202-0-1 when leading by 14 or more points in the fourth quarter at home in their history, including the postseason, according to ESPN.

On Sunday, the Cowboys led 24-10 with 14:20 remaining in regulation.

It matched the largest blown fourth-quarter lead in team history. In 2011 and 2022, the Cowboys blew fourth-quarter leads at the Jets and at the Packers, respectively. They are now 342-3-1 in franchise history when leading by at least 14 points in the fourth quarter.

Owner Jerry Jones called in “an indictment of the whole show.”

“We had numerable chances to win this game and didn’t do it,” Jones said. “And I know everybody . . . is disappointed. We came out the second half and were a shadow of ourselves. So there’s nothing to point to other than we just weren’t a good team in the second half.”

The Cowboys became the first team in the NFL this season to lose when leading by at least 14 points in the fourth. Teams were 44-0-1 in that situation entering Sunday.

#2744. Baker Mayfield sounds off on Buccaneers defeating Falcons with zero pass completions

The Tampa Bay Buccaneers have won their past two games with a dominant ground attack.

The Buccaneers are now 3-5 after knocking out the Atlanta Falcons in a dominant 16-0 victory over their NFC South rivals. The win not only put them ahead of the Falcons in the division, but also moved them a half game behind the 3-4 Carolina Panthers, whom they beat last week, for the NFC South lead.

This time they did it behind zero completions from Baker Mayfield on just three pass attempts. The Buccaneers became the first team since 1974 to win an NFL game with zero pass completions. They rode their rushing attack, with a franchise-record 324 rushing yards, to victory.

"It's winning, that's what I think about it -- we won," said Mayfield after the game. "Getting guys lined up, making sure we're running the right run plays. Obviously, ball security in these conditions. We had some early ones. Decided to go to the shotgun and pistol sets, just easier to receive the snaps instead of it coming back through your hands under center. So going from there and just really trying to manage the game and time management, trying to bleed as much clock as possible. Just get everybody on the same page and go from there. So that's my job in these conditions. And listen, I'll do whatever it takes to win. That's all that matters to me."

Over the past two weeks, the Buccaneers have completed just seven of their 14 pass attempts for 64 passing yards, with 582 rushing yards en route to victory. They've defeated the top two NFC South teams, 59-13 combined.

For a team that was just 1-5 a couple of weeks prior, the Buccaneers are suddenly back in the driver's seat to potentially win the NFC South for the fifth time in the past six seasons.

Tampa Bay will look to ride that momentum when they take on one of the NFC's best teams, the Chicago Bears, in a Sunday Night Football road matchup next week.

#2743. 10 thoughts on the Cowboys loss to the Cardinals

Wow. It's hard being a fan of the Dallas Cowboys these days, and those difficulties reached a new level after an indescribable 33-30 overtime loss to the Arizona Cardinals. While most of us were guarded against these pesky Cardinals due to the history between these teams, our guard was lowered just long enough to raise our hopes so they could be snatched away yet again. This one was a tough one, and here are 10 thoughts on this really sad Sunday morning showing.

Another game against Arizona, another loss. It's just not in the cards. For reasons as mysterious as the Loch Ness monster, the Cowboys cannot beat this football team. Even when it looks like the Cardinals are dead in the water, they find a way to rise up and defeat Dallas. The losing streak now sits at five straight and nine of the last 10 games. It's frustrating, it's peculiar, and it's downright tiring.

What's even weirder about this loss is that so many things went in the Cowboys' favor. They won the turnover battle, they won the penalty battle, and when loose balls were flying around, they were landing in the Cowboys' hands. Jonathan Mingo muffed a punt. No problem. Javonte Williams fumbled in the end zone. Don't fret; still a touchdown. Early in the game, the Cardinals receivers were dropping passes left and right, and it just felt like everything was working in the Cowboys' favor. Little did we know what lay ahead.

When the Cowboys get backed up deep in their own territory, they love to waste a down and QB-sneak it. They did it last week against the Eagles, and they did it again on Sunday. Both times resulted in a quick possession, as the Cowboys were forced to punt. Brian Schottenheimer clearly values safety over extending the drive. His team. His choice. If he likes to sneak so much, then why didn't he do so when he decided to go for it on 4th-and-inches at his own 30-yard line? Instead, he opted to run, and Williams was stuffed behind the line of scrimmage.

The playcalling was weird sometimes, but some of the logic behind the Cowboys' choices was equally puzzling. Going for it at your own 30-yard line is certainly a choice. In that moment, he chose to be aggressive. We get it. That's what makes his other passive moments really confusing. Late in the first half, the Cowboys had a shot at a field goal, and they chose to run the ball to get a little closer for Brandon Aubrey, but even still, it was a 60+ yard field goal attempt? Just because he's capable of booming those kicks doesn't mean you shouldn't at least try to get closer. It didn't seem like a whole lot at the time, but those three points would've come in handy later.

The Cardinals aren't viewed as a strong offensive team, but for the Cowboys to still hold them to just three points in the first half was impressive, especially considering the Dallas offense turned the ball over on downs in their own territory. Nice recovery, defense. But as good as they were in the first half, they were equally disastrous in the second half. They surrendered four second-half touchdowns, including three in the fourth quarter alone. The defense allowed two 50+ yard runs from Tyler Allgeier and couldn't make a stop to save their lives. It was a complete meltdown.

Despite the late comeback, the Cowboys still had a chance to ice the game. After a failed onside kick, Dallas was sitting in great shape. All they needed was one first down, and the game was over. The Cardinals only had one timeout left, and Mike LaFleur opted to use it on the plus side of the two-minute warning after a running play that went nowhere. This dared the Cowboys to pass on second down because the clock would stop after the next play no matter what. Dallas took the bait; only Prescott took the conservative approach and cautiously fell into a sack after his first read wasn't there. This resulted in a sack and gave them no chance to get a first down and run out the clock.

After the Cardinals scored a touchdown with just six seconds left, the life was sucked out of AT&T Stadium. The only thing left was for Arizona kicker Chad Ryland to hit the extra point and leave Dallas with another victory. Shockingly, he shanked it, missing his first extra point since 2024, and giving the Cowboys another chance they didn't deserve.

Despite transforming into a red-carpet defense in the second half, the Cowboys surprisingly forced the Cardinals to go three-and-out in their first possession of overtime. It set up a perfect opportunity for the Cowboys' offense to take control of the game and move into Aubrey range for the game-winner. They never got close. The offense's final possession was pathetic. It was a quick three-and-out, and they went backwards. The Cowboys punted the ball away and never got a chance again. The defense just didn't have it in them to make another stop.

It feels less exhilarating now, but there was a time when it was exciting to see Jacoby Brissett repeatedly succumb to pressure. The Cowboys sacked the Cardinals' quarterbacks five times, with two coming from Quinnen Williams, and one each from Donovan Ezeiruaku, Von Miller, and James Houston. Defensive tackle Elijah Garcia almost had another one, but Brissett was able to get rid of it at the last second. While most of the damage happened in the first half, it was good to see the Cowboys' pass rush show some life.

Entering the game, Brissett remained the only quarterback from Prescott's draft class in 2016 whom the Cowboys have yet to beat. They have faced seven quarterbacks from that draft, including Jared Goff, Carson Wentz, Cody Kessler, Nate Sudfeld, Brandon Allen, Jeff Driskel, and Brissett. All of them have fallen to the Cowboys at some point over the years, with the exception of Brissett, and it looked like they would finally be able to check him off the list as well. They had his number so well that he was benched and replaced with quarterback Gardner Minshew. The veteran came to the rescue and kept Brissett's winning streak against Dak and the Cowboys alive and well.

#2742. How Joe Mazzulla found a ‘leadership opportunity’ to test Celtics’ trust vs. Magic

Joe Mazzulla had a decision to make at the start of the fourth quarter against the Orlando Magic. Rather than disrupt his team's momentum, he chose to let the non-Jayson Tatum lineup ride it out.

Mazzulla substituted Luka Garza for Neemias Queta 12 seconds into the quarter, leaving Garza, Paul George, Payton Pritchard, Derrick White, and Baylor Scheierman on the floor. In less than four minutes, that group forced three turnovers, outscored the Magic 8-3, and prompted an Orlando timeout, extending Boston's lead to 85-79.

Mazzulla considered the early fourth quarter Boston's "sweet spot" and a valuable chance to test his leaders.

"It's always a balance," Mazzulla told reporters after Sunday night's 108-97 win, per NBC Sports Boston. "You wanna get those guys back in. But at the same time we're playing really, really well. So we're in that sweet spot, and I kind of wanted to ride those guys, and it's a leadership opportunity for Neemi and JT in those moments to let those guys play."

Mazzulla waited until nearly eight minutes had burned, reinserting Tatum and Queta with 4:22 remaining. By then, the Celtics had built a 97-91 cushion and still had some work to do. But Mazzulla's decision had paid off. The George, Pritchard, White, Scheierman and Garza lineup had a chance to step up in the first night of a back-to-back on the road, and they didn't abuse it. Those guys earned every minute, and Mazzulla wanted to make sure they felt rewarded.

Garza played a season-high 21 minutes off the bench, filling in for Mitchell Robinson's absence (rest). In the second quarter, Garza knocked down his first corner 3-pointer — the second Celtics make from beyond the arc in 16 attempts — to give the Celtics a 31-29 lead. He finished with 12 points, six rebounds (two offensive) and four assists, maximizing his time on the floor.

During that early fourth-quarter run, Garza assisted George, nailed his second corner three, and grabbed an offensive rebound before returning to the bench.

Garza pointed right at a member of the Orlando crowd after the three and pumped up his teammates.

"It's really just about knowing that the guys have each other's back and pick the guy up next to you," Mazzulla said. "That non-Tatum lineup was tremendous. We just have to continue getting better. They got us into that spot, and then the guys came back in and closed it out. So it's just about having each other's back in those moments."

For the first time this season, Mazzulla couldn't lean on Robinson for minutes. Instead, he utilized the team's depth to fend off a feisty Magic team that shot 35.9 percent from 3-point range to Boston's uncharacteristic 27.3 percent.

Although the Celtics struggled to find their rhythm from beyond the arc, they compensated with a strong effort on the other end to keep Orlando in check throughout the game.

"Defensively, we can always bring our defense, right?" George told reporters, per NBC Sports Boston. "We can always bring the intensity. We can always challenge guys. We can always pressure. We can always be disruptive. That's the part we should always bring night in, night out. And I thought that's what we did."

The Celtics were shorthanded, but not disadvantaged.

Similar to last season's team, George already sees the "togetherness" that carries over onto the court. No clashing personalities or individual agendas are getting in the way of what this group is built to accomplish. Everyone has an opportunity to shine, and when that moment arrives, the rest of the team is there to support them every step of the way.

That could look different any given night, depending on the circumstances Mazzulla and the coaching staff are tasked with navigating from the sidelines. But on Sunday night, the decision to entrust and empower the Tatum-less lineup was telling of where the Celtics are this early into the season.

"We were united out there," George added.

Six games in, Boston has won its last five straight — an NBA best mark.

#2740. Luka Doncic Posts Historic Statline to Lift Lakers Over Raptors

With the Los Angeles Lakers in need of a bounce-back win after falling to the Golden State Warriors to open the Emirates NBA Cup group play stage, superstar Luka Doncic set the tone defensively and filled up the stat sheet Sunday night.

Welcoming in the Toronto Raptors two nights after a 112-95 road loss to the Warriors, the Lakers turned to their unquestioned leader to get back in the win column. It would prove to be an all-around performance from Doncic in front of the hometown crowd. And despite a late rally by the Raptors, the Lakers move to 5-2 on the season behind Doncic's 45 points, 15 rebounds, six assists, five steals and a block in a 131-125 home win.

"Obviously, I'm not the best defender in the NBA. But I think this year I've really taken a step forward," Doncic proudly proclaimed after the win. "Obviously, people are going to talk what they want to talk. The media is going to talk what they want to talk, but I know, and my team knows that I think I'm better this year."

Los Angeles Lakers center Walker Kessler (14) high-fives guard Luka Doncic (77) during the second half of the game against the Toronto Raptors at Crypto.com Arena.

Doncic set the tone from the opening tipoff Sunday night at both ends of the floor in the first quarter. After 12 minutes of play, the Lakers led the Raptors by 13, 36-23, behind Doncic's 16 points on 5-of-7 shooting and 4-for-5 from three-point range, and recorded four rebounds, three assists, four steals, and a block in the period. In the process, Doncic became the first player in NBA history to record four steals and make four 3-pointers in the opening quarter.

By halftime, Doncic became the first NBA player in the play-by-play era (since 1997-98) to record 20 points, 5 rebounds, 5 3-pointers, and 5 steals in a half.

Doncic is the only player to record 45 points, 15 rebounds, 6 assists, 5 steals, and make 8 3-pointers in a game. Doncic is also the first player to record at least 15 rebounds, 5 assists, 5 steals, and 5 3-pointers in a game. He now also holds the record for the most games in Lakers franchise history with at least eight 3-pointers in a game, producing his sixth such night on Sunday to surpass the five by the legendary Kobe Bryant.

But perhaps Doncic's biggest impact was on the defensive end Sunday night.

Doncic made more history by the end of the night, becoming the first player to record five steals and three charges drawn in the same game since player tracking began in the 2013-14 season. Meanwhile, all 15 of Doncic's rebounds were on the defensive end. It's that defensive activity that Lakers coach JJ Redick highlighted after the game. And according to Redick, Doncic's increased defensive intensity boosts the rest of the team.

"He's been awesome on defense," Redick said of Doncic's defensive activity this season. "I think even just his on-ball (defense) throughout this early stretch of games has been really good just in terms of containment. You know, we show a lot of clips defensively (in film), and we try to highlight when guys communicate — when guys are pointing, when guys are talking.

"Again, it's 'cause he's been with us; this is his third season with us, " Redick continued. "You know, we pause it at halftime or pause it in the postgame review. He's doing a great job talking on defense beyond just the steals and the charges and the rebounding.

Still, it's the offensive end of the floor that will garner the most attention for Doncic after he led the NBA with 33.5 points per game last season. Early this season,

Doncic is averaging 37.7 points per game. That's the fifth-most in NBA history through six games and the most since Hall of Famer Michael Jordan during the 1986-87 campaign. Doncic now has the second-most games in NBA history with at least 45 points and five steals, trailing only Jordan in that department.

Doncic also has the most points per game through six games by any Laker ever, passing his own mark set last season. That is no surprise to Redick, who watched Doncic go on a similar roll before suffering a Grade 2 hamstring injury that ended his season in April.

"It feels pretty normal. I mean, we got to witness it for a month last year, and it was like a supernova. You know, it was loud. It feels loud right now," Redick said of Doncic's offensive explosion this season.

The Lakers will try to keep the momentum going Monday when they host the new-look Miami Heat on the second night of a back-to-back. Led by Doncic, the Lakers are shooting 51.2 percent from the field, the NBA's best mark. The team is also shooting 38.9 percent from three-point range, which ranks fourth in the league. The Lakers are averaging 120.3 points per game, ranking No. 5 in the league. That success has them tied for second in the NBA with an offensive rating of 123.3.

#2739. Twitter Gold: The Legend Of Spud

For people in the Triangle, it may come as a big surprise that people in the NBA didn't know that Spud Webb could jump.

People in the Triangle knew. We heard the stories first, that this 5-7 kid from Midland Junior College could really get up off the ground, but no one understood that his vertical might be as high as 47". That, combined with his insane quickness, made him a real threat.

But he was still 5-7, and there have only been a handful of NBA players that small who had significant careers. Think Earl Boykins and Muggsy Bogues, or Wat Misaka, the first non-Caucasian to play in the NBA (Misaka, who grew up in Utah, didn't actually have a great NBA career, but he did have an extraordinary journey. He was a talented guard who played college basketball when many Japanese-Americans were forced into internment camps, and went on to help Utah win the 1944 NCAA tournament. He was heavily booed through most of his college career. It's a fascinating story).

Once he got to the NBA, Webb legendarily won the NBA Dunk Contest as a rookie.

In this video, you'll get an idea of just how unusual he was, and how much of an impact he made. He was a huge amount of fun to watch.

#2736. Open Thread: Inside the NBA’s Ernie Johnson announces this is his final season

For thirty-eight years, Inside the NBA has been a staple of basketball analysis. In its premiere season, the show had no dedicated host. The following year, sideline reporter Ernie Johnson claimed the position as the show's host, a role he has maintain ever since.

Last week, the emcee and ringleader tasked with managing the personalities of Shaquille O'Neal, Charles Barkley, and Kenny "The Jet" Smith disclosed that the 2026-2027 season will be his last with the show. The announcement was immediately met with sorrow from the trio of retired players for which he's shared the broadcast over the years.

Johnson began his broadcasting career while attending the University of Georgia. A year after graduating, he worked as a newscaster in Macon, Georgia. Two years later he moved to South Carolina on general assignment, eventually picking up sports on the weekend.

From 1993-1996, Johnson called Atalanta Braves games alongside his father, a 1950s Major League pitcher and Braves play-by-play announcer from 1962-1999.

But E.J.'s bread-and-butter has been at the helm of Inside the NBA for over three decades. The steady hand, the voice of reason, and the man who has attempted for literally thousands of episodes to keep the train on the tracks. The show known for its chemistry and hijinks, highs and lows, and which, at times, seems to be less about basketball and more about the moment has engulfed the zeitgeist and become a staple of basketball. Whether it's the analysis, the banter, sense of humor (Charles Barkley picks on San Antonio as a town quite a bit), or political commentary (Kenny Smith walked off the set in response to the shooting of Jacob Blake), Inside the NBA has embraced fans worldwide.

When the show lost its broadcasting rights, Barkley walked away from an estimated $100 million to stay, saving the jobs of production and behind-the-scenes staff at Turner. In 2025, rather than being cancelled, Inside the NBA transitioned to ESPN and ABC while continuing to be produced by TNT Sports with the original crew.

The show has survived the slings and arrows. But one thing is for sure — once Ernie Johnson unplugs his microphone it will never be the same.

#2735. Bears at Seahawks Monday Night Football betting odds, picks and predictions: Best bets, player props

To the victors go the spoils, and back-to-back-back prime-time games.

The Seahawks took home Super Bowl LX to the "12s," but after the traditional, banner-raising opener at home on the first night of the season, it took awhile for the defending champs to get back on one of the NFL's three prime-time center stages.

Once they did, the Seahawks exemplified what makes the NFL — and betting it — so fascinating. On "Thursday Night Football" in Week 6, Sam Darnold's two crucial interceptions in a loss to Denver sent the talking heads into a fury about, "what's wrong with Seattle?"

A week-and-a-half later, on "Sunday Night Football," the Seahawks — specifically, the defense — performed about as well as they ever have, shutting down the Chiefs en route to a 20-3 home win, and, just like that, "the champs are back!"

Next up, a Monday nighter against another prime-time regular — the Bears — and the betting market has bounced back from brief concern to open Seattle at -3.5. Over the course of last week, that line has leveled off, sitting right on the biggest key number in NFL betting.

What do we mean when we talk about the belief in Seattle returning in the betting market?

To break it down quantitatively, the Seahawks got to a point at the end of last season and the beginning of this one, where if you gave them a power rating out of 100 (as we do at THE WINDOW), they were rated in the low-70s, among the top teams in the NFL.

After the loss to the Broncos, they were downgraded into the high-60s for last week's game against the Chiefs, with a closing line of -3 (just a point better than Kansas City plus two points of home-field advantage in Seattle).

Offensively, it remained a struggle, with Sam Darnold connecting with MVP candidate Jaxon Smith-Njigba for a pair of big catches, one for the key touchdown in a low-scoring game.

Defensively, the Seahawks played the best they had all season, focusing on former teammate, Kenneth Walker — the only concerning weapon in Patrick Mahomes' arsenal.

That was enough to shoot the Seahawks back up into the 70s in our estimated market ratings, jumping the Rams and Bills as the No. 1-rated team in the betting market (though not the Super Bowl favorite, because of where they stand behind the 49ers in the NFC West). The toggle between those two ratings means we've found the Seahawks' ceiling in the market.

Caleb Williams is back and in fine form, so the Bears bring a far more dangerous offense to Seattle, and their power rating of 68/100 might have more room to run upward. Especially, if the much-maligned defense can continue to create opportunities for Kyler Gordon (4.0 sacks already from slot-corner, going from 17 to 31 snaps in his first two games this season), and if newly acquired Jeffery Simmons is the same impact player with the Bears as he has been his whole career with the Titans.

Bet the Chicago Bears to cover the spread at sportsbooks right now

Add in that Seattle will be without offensive tackle Charles Cross and WR Rashid Shaheed, and the defense might need to keep the Bears offense in the single-digits, too. That seems almost impossible for the combo of a healthy Williams and Ben Johnson.

Caleb Williams over 20.5 pass completions (+100, Bet365)

Nothing comes easy against the Seahawks' defense, but it doesn't have to, on the way to 21 completions (or more).

As the most recent Super Bowl MVP can attest, running into the Seahawks' front doesn't produce much efficiency at all, but the Bears have enough options in the passing game that Chicago will likely have to move the ball in the air in the form of quick throws. If Seattle gets a lead, that will only force the passing urgency from Williams.

Tory Horton longest reception over 14.5 receiving yards (-110, DraftKings)

The Seahawks are desperate for another receiver to provide a threat across from Smith-Njigba. Shaheed was providing something of an occasional deep threat, catching a pass of at least 20 yards in four of his last five games before getting hurt.

With Shaheed out, Horton, who was already creeping close to playing 50% of the snaps the last two games, will get those routes down the field opposite JSN, with Cooper Kupp still manning the underneath.

With the Bears' safeties occasionally vulnerable deep passes, and Horton's five receptions on the season creating a lower betting line than you'd see on Shaheed, there's some value on Horton to capitalize on one good look from one of the better deep-ball throwers in the game.

Zach Charbonnet under 46.5 rushing + receiving yards (-115, Bet365)

Even before his ACL injury in the playoffs last season, Zach Charbonnet had fewer than 40 rushing yards nine times in the regular season, as he split the carries with Walker. In his absence, Emanuel Wilson has been better than serviceable, and first-round pick, Jadarian Price is expected to come off Injured Reserve on Monday, creating a suddenly crowded backfield for Seattle.

Never a big threat in the passing game, and other options more suited to third-down work, let's take the under here and see if Charbonnet already emerges as a workhorse against the Bears' bolstered defensive line.

CHICAGO, ILLINOIS - OCTOBER 22: D'Andre Swift #4 of the Chicago Bears runs with the ball against the New England Patriots during a game at Soldier Field on October 22, 2026 in Chicago, Illinois.

Kyle Monangai is out for the fourth straight game, and with the perception that the Seahawks defense doesn't give up touchdowns, there's the right combination of opportunity for Swift as the focal point (having scored in all three games without Monangai), and a decent price for a featured tailback.

With four catches in each of the past three games, a receiving touchdown is also in play more than usual.

The Bears aren't without their injuries, as TE Cole Kmet is out too, which means it's going to be harder to play the Seahawks defense with two-tight end sets.

Colston Loveland is going to get a ton of attention. Plus, the word is out on the impact of Luther Burden III.

#2731. Carrick in the dark over his future ahead of week of reckoning at Man United

With Manchester United on its worst run of results in nearly 40 years, Michael Carrick isn't looking beyond the upcoming week amid fevered speculation about his future.

Carrick is limping on as United manager amid a nine-game winless streak in all competitions that has featured desperate performances, critical post-match outbursts and audible fan disgruntlement toward the team's underperforming players.

A two-week international break, starting next Monday, is fast approaching and looks an ideal time for United to make decision on whether Carrick is still the man for the job.

Before then, United plays Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday and Aston Villa in the Premier League on Sunday.

"I don't know what's going to happen," said Carrick, sounding very much like someone not in charge of his own destiny.

Whatever happens, Carrick wants to go out with a bang — beginning with the visit of Roma in a fixture that holds sweet memories for him. Back in 2007, when United was one of Europe's top teams and Carrick was bestriding its midfield, he scored twice in a 7-1 rout of the Italian club in the second leg of the Champions League quarterfinals.

No wonder some enthusiasm was heard in his voice ahead of the game at Old Trafford.

"You may think I'm crazy with the results we've had and what's going on," Carrick said, "but I genuinely really can't wait for the game tomorrow. That is what I'm focused on. I really am.

"Whatever happens is going to happen after that, in whatever direction it goes in. But we want to make it a big night tomorrow night first."

Carrick said the United locker room "is a good place," despite the club's longest winless run since 1988 and the fact that the once-feared Red Devils are in 17th place in the Premier League — only out of the relegation zone on goal difference — and 20th in the 36-team Champions League standings.

"The commitment of the players to the club, to me, to each other, I don't question that at all," Carrick said. "We need to play better, we can make better decisions, but the commitment is not a thing at all."

Nowhere is the scrutiny stronger than on Lisandro Martinez, the Argentina defender who blasted club officials in media interviews after last month's Champions League loss at Atletico Madrid and then collected two yellow cards in four minutes in an act of self-destruction that led to United losing 2-0 at Chelsea on Saturday.

Carrick refused to even look at Martinez as the defender walked off the field following his red card. Yet, it doesn't appear he has given up on him just yet.

"I've got no concerns about the commitment at all," Carrick said of Martinez. "Things happen in football — sometimes you do things, sometimes you make a decision, sometimes you make mistakes, sometimes it goes well for you. The commitment is not an issue for sure."

With just over a week to go until the NFL trade deadline, attention will inevitably turn to the usual question: What will the Jets do?

On the face of it, the situation is relatively straightforward. With a 2-6 record after Sunday's loss to the Las Vegas Raiders, the Jets are all but out of the postseason mix. Speculation is already underway, with players like Breece Hall, Garrett Wilson, and Will McDonald among those discussed as potentially being movable.

Any moves that bring in draft pick compensation, or create cap room, could give the front office more to work with in terms of putting the 2027 roster together. In addition, if losing some of their current contributors makes the team less competitive and leads to New York getting a higher draft pick in April, some wouldn't see it as a bad thing.

But is there an argument to be made that the Jets would be be better off not doing anything?

Offloading talent was the approach New York took last season when they dealt Sauce Gardner and Quinnen Williams. As a result, they already have plenty of draft compensation to head into this offseason with, and they have a healthy cap situation, too.

Thinking ahead, if the Jets are going to be active in the free agent market this offseason, it might be hard to attract talent if they continue to perpetuate the image of a team that can't compete and can't hold onto their talent.

Perhaps more importantly, if the Jets are going to draft their quarterback of the future in April as is widely expected, then they arguably shouldn't make any moves that downgrade their offensive personnel.

If that rookie passer can step into a lineup with an established offensive line that has played together as a group and – by recent standards – an embarrassment of riches at the skill positions, it could create a situation that breeds early success.

In the case of players like Hall, Wilson, and McDonald, the temptation to move them makes sense on some level. Each of them plays a position where a young player has stepped up in recent weeks. Braelon Allen has regularly rushed for 100 yards with Hall out and Omar Cooper Jr. had back-to-back 100-yard games, while Wilson's target share was down in recent weeks and David Bailey has outproduced McDonald, cutting into his playing time.

The Jets have been clear that they have no intention of trading Wilson, and Hall is still here after similar trade speculation over the past few seasons. And Hall's market will presumably shrink if the Colts trade Jonathan Taylor.

Aug 14, 2026; East Rutherford, New Jersey, USA; New York Jets running back Breece Hall (20) carries the ball against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the first half at MetLife Stadium. / John Jones-Imagn Images

If the Jets were going to move one of these three, McDonald would make the most sense because trading him wouldn't downgrade the offensive personnel heading into next season. However, the recent injuries on the defensive line underscore how important depth is at the NFL level, and the Jets would probably be selling low on McDonald, whose value may have fallen due to an unproductive first half of the season.

The importance of carrying over as much depth as possible into 2027 was also underlined by Allen limping off with an injury with the Raiders game still in the balance.

While Allen returned, it illustrates that if the Jets traded Hall they could find themselves in an important game next season where they end up forced to rely on someone inexperienced because Allen gets banged up.

The recent success of the Detroit Lions, which head coach Aaron Glenn saw firsthand when he was their defensive coordinator, shows how effective a two-headed monster can be. Indeed, Glenn's former colleague Ben Johnson is now having similar success with the same approach in Chicago.

Nobody can be sure of how secure Glenn and Darren Mougey's futures are, and how involved ownership might be in any decisions currently being made. But everyone should be more or less on the same page. It may be that the Jets try to remain as competitive as possible for the remainder of the season, so they have something to build on next year, as opposed to tearing things down and starting over from the ground up.

With the Jets, nothing can ever be ruled out. Twelve years ago, the team was off to an even worse start than this season, losing six of their first seven games. However, they still felt they had a chance to get back into the playoff mix, so they traded a 2015 pick for wide receiver Percy Harvin.

More recently, they were 2-4 and had lost three straight when they traded for Davante Adams in 2024.

These moves made no difference, but if the current decision makers still believe in their team and feel like they need to keep competing for the good of their own job security, there are certainly areas of the team that could be upgraded.

There may be a middle ground that involves making one or two less significant moves, perhaps with a young player returning to the Jets to audition for a role -- similar to the trades that were made last season.

Ultimately, though, if the deadline comes and goes with high levels of speculation but no actual moves, there may at least be some logic behind that approach.

#2728. Ducks match Leo Carlsson's $90 million offer sheet: Anaheim star tops list of NHL's highest-paid players

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Anaheim Ducks didn't need the full seven days to decide whether to match the Philadelphia Flyers' record five-year, $90 million offer sheet to Leo Carlsson. Just a few days after Carlsson signed the Flyers' offer, the Ducks announced that they had matched the deal, keeping the Swedish center in Anaheim and making him the highest-paid player in NHL history.

Philadelphia rocked the hockey world last week when they signed Carlsson, and the $18 million AAV was lofty enough that there was uncertainty about whether Anaheim would match the deal. The Ducks could've let Carlsson walk and taken four first-round picks from the Flyers, but they chose to keep their franchise cornerstone instead.

The No. 2 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Carlsson is still blossoming into a superstar No. 1 center. He took a big step in that direction last season when he posted 29 goals and 38 assists in 70 games. Perhaps more importantly, Carlsson's five-on-five game showed major improvement as the Ducks controlled 53.4% of the expected goals with him on the ice, per Natural Stat Trick.

Carlsson still has work to do in order to become an $18 million player, but he's on the right track. Even if Carlsson doesn't quite get all the way there, he should come close, and the rising salary cap will take away some of the sticker shock over the next several years.

Still, the Ducks were in a legitimate bind, and they still are to a certain degree. After Carlsson signed his offer sheet, Anaheim wanted to avoid a similar situation with 22-year-old defenseman Pavel Mintyukov, so the team locked him in on a five-year, $36 million deal. Mintyukov is a gifted player, but he has very real holes in his game defensively, so that was a desperate gamble on the part of the Ducks.

Now, Anaheim has just over $9 million in salary cap space and another major restricted free agent to sign. Cutter Gauthier, 22, just posted a 41-goal season and needs a new contract. His annual number will almost certainly come in over $10 million, so the Ducks have some maneuvering to do, and that doesn't even take into account the fact that the team doesn't even have six NHL-caliber defensemen on the roster.

Pat Verbeek still has a lot of work ahead of him, but at least he knows his best player is signed through the next five seasons. Now he just needs to figure out what to do with the pieces around Carlsson.

This contract makes Carlsson the highest-paid player in NHL history on an annual basis. He topped Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov's record ($17 million), which was set last summer.

That puts a lot of pressure on Carlsson to perform as a true superstar because players making several million dollars less than him already have Hart Trophy wins, Rocket Richard trophies and Stanley Cup rings. Some of that is simply timing. As the salary cap rises, contracts explode, and Carlsson just happens to be latest star player to get a new deal.

When Auston Matthews and Connor McDavid sign new contracts in a couple of years, their annual salaries will rival or surpass that of Carlsson. That said, heavy is the head that wears the crown, and the Ducks are counting on Carlsson to step into an elite tier moving forward.

There are a few players who could join this list in short order. Connor Bedard is still a restricted free agent -- and despite his recent shoulder injury, he should still get a hefty payday from the Chicago Blackhawks. Plus, superstar defensemen Cale Makar and Quinn Hughes are eligible for extensions, and those contracts will reset the market for that position.

#2727. Greg Rousseau passes Darryl Talley, with Mario Williams next in his sights

Greg Rousseau has another milestone to add to his growing résumé with the Buffalo Bills. The outside linebacker recorded a sack against the Baltimore Ravens giving him 39 for his career and moving him past Darryl Talley into eighth place on the franchise's all-time sack list.

Talley spent 12 seasons in Buffalo and was part of the Bills teams that went to four consecutive Super Bowls in the early 1990s. He finished his time with the team with 38.5 sacks in 188 regular-season games. Rousseau, meanwhile, needed just 85 games to move past that total. Not bad for a player who is only in his sixth NFL season.

And this season, Rousseau has been making that climb a little faster. With Jim Leonhard taking over as defensive coordinator under new head coach Joe Brady, Rousseau has moved from defensive end to outside linebacker. The change has given him different opportunities to get after opposing quarterbacks, and the results have been hard to miss. Rousseau recorded two sacks in each of Buffalo's first three games before being held without one against New England.

He entered Monday night's game with six sacks, already within reach of the career-high eight he recorded in both 2022 and 2024. Now, with Talley behind him on the leaderboard, Rousseau has another name to chase. Mario Williams, who played four seasons in Buffalo from 2012 through 2015, sits seventh with 43 sacks.

#2726. Giants star nearly quit football. His NFL journey started in NJ | Exclusive

EAST RUTHERFORD - Jermaine Eluemunor used to take umbrage with those who tried to belittle his talent by calling him a journeyman offensive lineman.

The NFL life that now has him at the top of his game has been all about the journey, man.

The New York Giants are in first place atop the NFC East standings, coming off their bye week in the aftermath of a dominant performance in Houston for Eluemunor, who went up against NFL sack leader Will Anderson Jr. and essentially erased him from the game in a 27-21 overtime victory over the Texans.

"I know I'm the best right tackle in the NFL, I do believe that and I think my play reflects that every week, but I do think about the twists and turns of my career all the time, especially with where we are at as a team," Eluemunor shared with NorthJersey.com and The Record last week, and his performances and blocking metrics over the past two seasons serve to support his assertion, too.

"I shouldn't be where I am. Six teams in 10 years? I sucked, so Baltimore traded me. When I was in New England, struggling with depression, I wanted to quit. When I was in Vegas, benched, wanted to quit. There was a game in Vegas where I gave up six sacks, almost quit there. When I got here, things really started to go well for me, but there were times last year when mentally, the game makes you think, how much do I want this anymore?"

He paused before adding: "You ask those questions, but then think about your goals, and your family, your kids, and you don't want to be seen as a quitter in their eyes. You want to make sure you set the example, and the standard is to strive to be the best at whatever you do. That becomes the motivation: being the best me I can be."

The reliability factor Eluemunor brings to the right side of the Giants' offensive line, pairing with cornerstone left tackle Andrew Thomas, is undeniable. He found the right team in the right offense and within a scheme that asks a lot out of the bookend tackles. Both Thomas (groin) and Eluemunor (calf) have been grinding for weeks prior to the bye week, and while the former was the No. 4 overall selection in the 2020 NFL Draft, the latter took quite a different path to get here.

Eluemunor is a cautionary tale in the NFL when it comes to any prospect, but offensive linemen in particular, and giving up on players too soon. Whether it's players giving up on themselves or teams giving up on young players too soon, there were far too many moments when Eluemunor could have thrown in the white flag, as noted above.

Through his struggles, the 6-foot-4, 338-pound Eluemunor felt small at times. He wondered if the work without the results was worth it, whether he could give much more. The quest is challenging enough, and Eluemunor was forced to adjust both physically and mentally. He had to be willing to strip down everything and build back up.

Eluemunor has a calming presence off the field and a fiery demeanor between the lines, adding stability and a steadiness to an offensive line that has been maligned for over a decade. He has constantly taken the field with an awareness that he could have been bounced out of the league a while ago for inconsistency, injury and erratic play.

He was praised as a rookie fifth-round draft pick of John Harbaugh's Ravens. Then he was dealt to New England.

And then he was released, also labeled a bust as the merry-go-round of the NFL started spinning.

Eluemunor started believing in himself again early in the 2022 season when he crossed paths with an opponent bound for Canton. "Hey, I love your film" is what J.J. Watt, then with the Arizona Cardinals, told Eluemunor on the field after they played in Week 2.

"That was the most unexpected thing ever. That was cool as hell," Eluemunor recalled. "To hear something like that from someone like J.J. Watt – a first-ballot future Hall of Famer – just makes you believe even more, and after that, I think I took my game to another level."

As a teenage athlete, Eluemunor believed in his potential. It's why he begged his parents to allow him to move from England to the United States at the age of 14. He recalls walking into the coaches' office at Morris Knolls High School in New Jersey and asking for a kit - another term for uniform in soccer and rugby, which he played growing up.

Ultimately, his size and athleticism allowed Eluemunor to excel in wrestling and football - even though he had very little experience in either sport. He wound up at at Lackawanna College, a JUCO in Scranton, Pa., where he felt the urgency and the desperation of a dream deferred. He had fallen in love with the idea of being in the NFL while watching his first game - Giants vs. Dolphins, the first London game in 2007 - and was certain regarding the future he wanted; the only mystery was how to achieve it.

"You definitely sensed the desperation, we knew what this opportunity meant to him," Lackawanna coach Mark Duda told NorthJersey.com and The Record in a 2024 interview. "You're in athletics long enough, you can tell when guys have 'it,' and Jermaine has it. We didn't know what he'd be able to turn that into, but he was so raw, he had a chance if he could put everything together. He worked so hard, there aren't many that we've had like him."

In one year of football at Lackawanna, Eluemunor went from essentially begging for a chance to being wanted - really, really wanted. He wound up at Texas A&M, but the journey - as has been the case his entire life - provided plenty of lessons and motivation along the way.

"I remember the first ever school that said they were interested in me was Akron, and I thought I was like a made man," Eluemunor said with a laugh. "Then the offers started to come: Florida State, Oregon, Oregon State, Georgia, Alabama, Wisconsin, Maryland, Rutgers. I remember Rutgers, emailing them the year prior and I was told I wasn't good enough for them. A year and a half later, all these schools wanted me, I think I had over 1,000 letters at my house. Life turned."

Bringing back the 31-year-old Eluemunor was a priority for Harbaugh and team brass this offseason. The Cleveland Browns and Kansas City Chiefs both made strong pushes to sway Eluemunor, but in the end, he reupped with the Giants on a three-year deal worth a maximum of $39 million, sources told NorthJersey.com and The Record at the time of signing.

"I understand the question of, 'Do guys get comfortable and maybe shut it down [when they get paid]?', and he's the opposite," Giants general manager Joe Schoen said when asked about Eluemunor last week. "He's had some nicks and dings here where you could have easily shut it down, and one thing about Jermaine is, he wants to be out there, and especially if it's going to be a Pro Bowl caliber or the highest paid at a position across from him. He really steps up to those challenges."

The Giants (4-2-1) return to the practice field Monday to begin preparation for this Sunday's game against the Eagles (2-6) in Philadelphia, where the franchise has not won since 2013. Then it's a quick turnaround for a Thursday night rematch of the overtime tie with the Washington Commanders (2-4-1) at MetLife Stadium on Nov. 12.

"Something has just clicked for me," Eluemunor said. "Because when you're at rock bottom, and you're trying to get to where you want to get to, and you don't quit, sometimes things just have a way of working out. The motivation is more than money now. I don't think I'd be here if I didn't have the will to be the best at my position. When I used to say that earlier in my career, people would laugh at me. There's not too much laughter anymore. I know how good I am, and I know how good I can be. We have big goals on this team, and I want to be a big part of helping achieve those goals. We're on this run together, and I feel like we're just getting started."

For Jermaine Eluemunor and the Giants, that improbable journey continues. The dreams are no longer deferred.

"Win the division, be an All-Pro, make a run. Maybe if I get five All-Pros in the next five years, we can talk about the Hall of Fame," Eluemunor added with a smile. "I know it sounds crazy, but goals are supposed to be crazy. Be confident in who you are, believe in yourself and who knows, you might just prove yourselves right on the way to the top."

#2725. What's next for Connor Bedard, Blackhawks after massive five-year, $75 million contract extension

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Chicago Blackhawks have locked in their franchise cornerstone for the near future. On Saturday, the Blackhawks announced that star center Connor Bedard has signed a five-year contract worth $75 million.

Bedard's $15 million average annual value makes him the third-highest paid player in the NHL for the 2026-27 season. Only Minnesota Wild winger Kirill Kaprizov ($17 million) and the newly-signed Anaheim Ducks center Leo Carlsson ($18 million) are ahead of him.

"Connor has continuously defied our expectations since being drafted, and has quickly established himself as an elite player in the NHL," Blackhawks general manager Kyle Davidson said in a statement. "He utilizes all aspects of his game to not only be a constant threat, but to make the players around him better every time he steps on the ice. Connor's strong work ethic and determination to always improve his game has set an extraordinary standard for our young core, and we're excited for the incredible impact he'll have in this next chapter of Blackhawks hockey."

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2023 NHL Draft, Bedard has already displayed elite offensive upside, even if his overall game still has work to do. Last season, Bedard posted a career high 75 points in 69 games. In 219 NHL games, Bedard has totaled 75 goals and 128 assists.

The biggest issues for Bedard are durability concerns -- he's played fewer than 70 games in two of three seasons and will miss the first month of the upcoming season with a shoulder injury -- and subpar defense. The defense is a common problem for young centers and should improve in the coming years, but Bedard has now suffered multiple shoulder injuries in his career.

With Bedard's long-term contract finalized, both he and the Blackhawks will try to take the next step toward greatness. For the player, that means refining his game in order to become the $15 million man most believe him to be. For the team, that means surrounding Bedard with an adequate supporting cast for the first time in his career.

First and foremost, Bedard needs to get healthy and stay healthy. After missing 13 games with a shoulder injury last year, Bedard suffered another injury that required surgery to fix, and he will miss roughly a dozen games out of the gate in 2026-27. Those issues may delay his jump into the NHL's elite tier of players.

Once back at full strength, Bedard will have to show improvement defensively. He oozes offensive ability, but if Bedard is going to be a true No. 1 franchise center, he has to thrive at both ends of the ice. With Bedard on the ice at five-on-five last season, Chicago surrendered 3.60 xGA/60, per Natural Stat Trick. That was the second-worst number on the team with rookie Anton Frondell bringing up the rear.

That doesn't necessarily mean Bedard was the Blackhawks' worst defensive player, but it does mean he often struggled when going up against the opposing team's best players. Stars -- especially those raking in $15 million per season -- are expected to drive play for their team regardless of circumstance. Bedard didn't do that last season.

Bedard also needs to show more growth in the face-off circle. To his credit, Bedard has already done that, going from 38.9% as a rookie to 47.1% last season. Still, Chicago would probably like to see Bedard closer to 50%, especially with him taking key draws in big moments. Maybe that number keeps rising as Bedard gets strong and adds more tricks in the dot.

If Bedard can round out his game without the puck, $15 million per season will be a very fair deal, especially as salaries explode across the league.

We've already seen what can happen when a restricted free agent has all the leverage in contract negotiations. The Ducks were essentially backed into a $90 million contract after the Philadelphia Flyers signed Carlsson to a massive offer sheet.

That risk was there for Bedard too, which is why Davidson deserves some credit for signing him at a more reasonable cap hit. Bedard still has work to do in order to reach that price point, but his ceiling is worth at least $15 million per season.

The Blackhawks can help their young star by putting more NHL-caliber players around him. Chicago tore it down to the studs in hopes of landing Bedard in the 2023 draft, and while that plan worked, it also created a roster full of holes around the No. 1overall pick. Over the last three seasons, Bedard has had little help.

Chicago already improved its defense this offseason when it acquired Bowen Byram from the Buffalo Sabres. Say what you will about the acquisition cost or his $75 contract extension, but Byram inarguably makes Chicago better on the blue line. That unit still needs work, but it's a step in the right direction.

The real issue is finding Bedard a quality running mate at the top of the lineup. Outside of Bedard, only one other player topped 50 points in 2025-26, and it was 31-year-old Tyler Bertuzzi. Chicago still has $14.1 million in cap space with which to add some firepower, but some upgrades will have to come internally.

It's conceivable that the Blackhawks' lineup will include seven players selected inside the top 50 picks of the last five drafts.

That's an exciting proposition, and fans have reasons to be optimistic about the future. That said, none of those players have really established themselves as future stars, outside of Bedard. Frondell, Nazar and Rinzel seem like the best bets to get there soon, but that's based more on projection than anything tangible.

The first month of the season should be an excellent barometer for the Blackhawks as they assess those players. Bedard will be out of the lineup, and it'll be interesting to see who sinks and who swims until he returns. Once Chicago establishes exactly what it has in its young nucleus, Davidson can then go out and aggressively address needs via trades and free agency.

#2724. 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Dolphins

It wasn't pretty, but the New England Patriots left Miami as winners and now sit at 5-3 for the season.

The team of head coach Mike Vrabel started slowly, and played some uninspired football in all three phases to start their Week 8 contest versus the Dolphins. Coming out of the half, however, they showed some much-needed urgency and scored 21 unanswered points to help secure a 24-19 victory.

Let's get into our lessons learned from the game.

Over the first 30 minutes on Sunday, the Patriots played arguably their worst half of football this season. Coming out of a mini-bye and against a one-win team, they went into the locker room down by 10 points, trailing 13-3. They then came out and scored three touchdowns before giving up a late score to the Dolphins the last time they had the ball.

The turnaround obviously changed the game, but it is also an indication of the mental toughness of this team.

They have consistently risen to the challenge and fought back, even when they have been struggling. With so many starters out, and another going down in this game — TE Hunter Henry — the Patriots never quit and did what they needed to do to come out of there with a win. It may not have been pretty, but a win is a win, and this was a huge one for the Patriots.

As poor as Drake Maye and the offense looked in the first two quarters, they, and he, played that well in the second half. The deep pass is still there, with a beautiful touchdown to Kyle Williams, and he also delivered a good throw off a fake pitch down the sideline to DeMario Douglas for another score.

Maye's move at the goal line to score a touchdown, meanwhile, was just slick. When he is feeling it, he's one of the best quarterbacks in the league. He certainly felt it over the last 30 minutes on Sunday.

No receivers, his favorite target goes out early in the game, the team is playing bad football, and he comes out of the half and leads the team to victory. When he is playing the way he was in the second half on Sunday, the Patriots can win any game anywhere under any circumstance.

Cory Durden stepped and played fantastic on Sunday. Not only did he have 1.5 sacks, but he was also a force in the run game as well. The Patriots have two very good defensive linemen already in Christian Barmore and Milton Williams, but are in need of someone else to help out. Durden did just that on Sunday.

He's far from a perfect player, but he has shown the potential to do what he did against Miami. If he does on a consistent basis, that would be a huge boost for the Patriots defensive line.

Speaking of helping the Patriots defense, Gabe Jacas is consistently putting together solid games. He has been very good against both the run and the pass this year, and he added another 1.5 sacks on Sunday. He's now up to three quarterback takedowns on the season, and is becoming a problem that other teams are going to have to answer for every weekend.

My favorite play of his was when he was in the backfield getting held, and helped force a loss anyway. He ended up leaving the game with a knee injury, so we'll have to see how healthy he is. Overall, though, he has looked very good this year and has been a real help for a Patriots defense that had significant questions on the edge entering the season.

With so many skill players on the offense out, the Patriots needed some guys to step up. A few of them did, in different ways.

Drake Maye's target with the most catches ended up being Efton Chism, who redeemed himself after his first-half fumble. The Patriots also got big plays from both Kyle Williams and DeMario Douglas, who both had touchdowns of 40-plus yards on the day.

Rhamondre Stevenson, however, ended up being the most reliable player on offense. He ran hard, as he always does, caught all three of his targets, and even closed out the game with a third-down carry for a first down. The Patriots need more of their players to get healthy, but in the second half on Sunday, they saw enough of their role players step up so that Stevenson and Maye could lead the offense to victory.

The Patriots have had a history of fantastic kickers. They had Adam Vinatieri and Stephen Gostkowski, who, when you combine their play, were top-tier players at the position for over 20 years. Even Nick Folk looked very good following in Gostkowski's shoes for a couple of seasons.

Now, they have a guy who currently isn't good enough. Andy Borregales is too inconsistent to be the kicker on a team that has deep playoff aspirations: through eight games, he has missed an extra point and three field goals, including a 40-yarder on Sunday.

Having a kicker like him is a recipe for disaster that could rear its ugly head at some point late in the season. Of course, he did manage to get out of a similar funk last year. If he can't break it this time around, however, the team should explore brining someone in on the practice squad to serve as emergency depth.

The Patriots love what they have gotten from Morgan Moses over the last year and a half. He's been a real leader in the locker room and a mentor for their young offensive linemen, including back-to-back first-round draft picks Will Campbell and Caleb Lomu. However, it looks like it might be time to hand over the job to Lomu.

Moses just doesn't appear to have the athleticism to play the position at a consistent level anymore. This might be because of the injury that he's been dealing with, but it doesn't matter. As much as you want to give the veterans a chance to play through their struggles, it seems that Lomu is better at the right tackle spot right now than Moses. It might be time let the kid take over.

It feels like the Patriots have suffered injuries to every starting unit on the field this year, and they had two more noteworthy ones on Sunday. Tight end Hunter Henry and edge Gabe Jacas both left the game with injuries.

Henry had a foot injury, and for Jacas it was a knee. The former tried to come back, but was unable to, while Jacas did not return at all. Dre'Mont Jones was also slow to get off the field at one point, and it feels like he's constantly a little banged up and playing through something.

There's a realistic chance that Mack Hollins will be coming off injured reserve soon, and we don't know how serious the injuries are to Jacas and Henry. Unfortunately, questions like these have become a weekly problem for the Patriots.

It seems like every week we see a fair share of questionable refereeing decisions, and this Sunday was no different. Now, that did not come unexpected, since the crew that worked the Patriots game was pulled off of Sunday Night Football game because of apparent poor performance.

It showed: ruling the Kyle Williams touchdown incomplete on the field made zero sense; there is simply no way that the ref standing there could think it was anything other than a touchdown.

It felt like they missed a bunch of other calls as well, including on an unnecessary roughness call against Christian Elliss and the fourth down to DeMario Douglas. The latter, like Williams' touchdown, was corrected upon review.

Still, all things considered the refs on Sunday were probably a half-step better than replacement refs. Something needs to change.

The Patriots have the Packers traveling to them next weekend for a 4:25 p.m. ET matchup at Gillette Stadium. The Packers, who have a mini-bye after beating the Panthers on Thursday, are a solid football team, even though they are currently in last place in a highly competitive NFC North.

Their offense has the potential to come alive at any moment, and the defense has played well in the last few weeks. For the Patriots to win, the key number will be 20.

The Packers have given up less than 20 points in all of their wins this season, and are 0-3 when they give up 20-plus. If the Patriots offense can get going, they should be able to top 20 points, and, hopefully the Packers will stay true to form.
