#2723. Jets star goalie Connor Hellebuyck requests trade: Where three-time Vezina Trophy winner could land

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After months of speculation about his future in Winnipeg, Jets goaltender Connor Hellebuyck has confirmed his trade request publicly.

Hellebuyck's name has come up in trade rumors since the 2025-26 season ended, and the rumor mill will only pick back up now that he's gone public with his request. NHL training camps will open soon, and Hellebuyck wanted to provide more clarity on the situation.

"Winnipeg has been home for my entire NHL career, and I will always be grateful for my time there.

"I have never forgotten June 23, 2012. That's the day Winnipeg took a chance on a goalie playing in Odessa, Texas. I gave everything I had from that moment to prove the Jets made the right decision.

"Several months ago, I privately requested a trade. I have tried to handle the situation quietly and respectfully while giving the organization time to explore its options.

"With training camp approaching, I felt it was important to publicly confirm my request. My position has not changed, and I believe moving on is the best path forward for me and my family.

"I appreciate everything Winnipeg Jets fans have meant to me throughout my career and hope a resolution can be reached soon."

In what would become one of the biggest steals in NHL Draft history, the Jets used the No. 130 overall pick to select Hellebucyk in 2012. Just seven years later, Hellebuyck established himself as one of the best goalies in the lea, and he's maintained that level of play for nearly a decade.

A three-time Vezina Trophy winner, Hellebuyck has a legitimate claim as the best goaltender in the world. Over the last three seasons, Hellebucyk has totaled 73.4 goals saved above average, per Natural Stat Trick. That's 20 more than the next closest goaltender -- Andrei Vasilevskiy -- and includes a rather underwhelming 2025-26 campaign.

There have been plenty of years in which Hellebuyck carried mediocre Jets teams, but 2025-26 was not one of them. He actually allowed 0.35 goals above average with a pedestrian 0.895 save percentage. Normally, it would be fair to worry about a 33-year-old goalie with those numbers, but not in Hellebucyk's case.

Hellebuyck backstopped Team USA to its first men's ice hockey gold medal in 46 years at the 2026 Olympics while allowing a total of six goals and boasting a .956 save percentage. He was exceptional in the final against Canada, where he turned away 41 of the 42 shots he faced and made one of the most iconic saves in hockey history.

THAT WAS ONE HELLE-BUYCK OF A STOP. 😳 pic.twitter.com/N3wCimdBGw

The biggest obstacle in a trade might be Hellebucyk's contract. He has five years remaining on his current deal at $8.5 million per season -- and while that may be a lot of term for a goalie his age -- Hellebucyk is worth a lot more than that at his best. The real issue is that he owns a full no-movement clause, which means Hellebuyck controls his fate, and the trade request going public certainly won't improve the team's leverage.

So, where does Hellebucyk land? Without knowing his preferred destinations, it's probably safe to assume that he wants the opportunity to win a Stanley Cup, and the team that acquires him will need the requisite cap space and resources to do so.

With those parameters in mind, here are five teams that could make sense as Hellebuyck trade suitors.

The Sabres were one of two teams frequently connected to Hellebuyck earlier in the offseason, and that makes sense. Buffalo is an ascending team with room to upgrade in the crease. Not to denigrate Alex Lyon and Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen, who were a formidable tandem in 2025-26, but I'm not sure Buffalo can bet on similar performances this upcoming season. Adding Hellebuyck would eliminate that question mark immediately and make the Sabres a favorite to win the Atlantic Division.

In fact, one of Luukkonen or Lyon could go back to Winnipeg to help provide stability in the post-Hellebuyck era. The Sabres also own all their first-round picks for the foreseeable future, and it would probably take at least two of those to pry Hellebuyck from the Jets. Just a year ago, it would be hard to believe that Hellebuyck would waive his no-movement clause to go to Buffalo, but it seems very plausible now.

When the Devils traded Jacob Markstrom to the Florida Panthers in July, I assumed it would only be a matter of time until Hellebuyck was in Newark. To this point, nothing has come to fruition, but New Jersey absolutely needs an NHL-caliber starter. Jake Allen, David Rittich and Nico Daws are on the roster right now, and that won't get the job done.

The Devils were undone by poor goaltending -- and subpar defense -- too much last year. Markstrom allowed 13.7 goals above average, per Natural Stat Trick, and even a diminished version of Hellebuyck would provide a significant upgrade over those numbers. New Jersey has the draft capital to get something done, but it also needs to clear cap space, possibly with a Dougie Hamilton salary dump.

They just won the Stanley Cup with Brandon Bussi in net, so the Hurricanes have proven they don't need elite goaltending to go all the way. Regardless, running it back with Bussi wouldn't be a very safe bet, and adding Hellebuyck would only reinforce Carolina's biggest strength. As we saw in the playoffs, the Hurricanes are already one of the best defensive teams in the league. Put Hellebuyck behind that lineup, and scoring on Carolina becomes a Herculean task.

Thanks to savvy cap management by GM Eric Tulsky, Carolina has the room to add Hellebuyck without jettisoning a current player. Oh, and Carolina has three first-round picks over the next two years. If Tulsky wants to pursue Hellebuyck, he has the resources to do it.

This is more of a longshot, but it would be fun to see the Sharks take a swing if this, assuming Hellebuyck would sign off on a trade to San Jose. Despite the fact that they overpaid for it, the Sharks blue line is better, and there is a wealth of young talent at forward. Another factor here is the current state of the Pacific Division, which is abhorrent. The third playoff spot is up for grabs, and the Sharks could secure it with Hellebuyck in goal.

Superstar Macklin Celebrini is on the final year of his entry-level deal before his $18.8 million salary kicks in next year, so San Jose needs to push the chips in here and figure out the finances next summer. Would the team be willing to trade blue-chip goaltending prospect Yaroslav Askarov to the Jets? San Jose may also need to sweeten a trade package -- or involve a third team -- in order to get Winnipeg to take on Logan Couture's contract.

Yes, Vegas is currently $8.6 million over the salary cap, so there would need to be some impressive maneuvering in order to acquire Hellebuyck. But the Golden Knights have already proven to be cutthroat if a player they covet hits the trade market. Besides, goaltending was optional in Sin City last season. Four goalies combined to allow 23.2 goals above average. Only five teams had a worse save percentage than the Golden Knights.

So, how could the Golden Knights pull off a Hellebuyck blockbuster? Trading an injured Alex Pietrangelo and his contract would help, but that may be costly. Veteran defenseman Brayden McNabb only has a modified no-trade clause, and the same is true for forwards Tomas Hertl, William Karlsson and Ivan Barbashev. Like I said, this would be tough, but the Golden Knights are one team willing to drop the entire egg carton on the floor to make a few omelettes.

#2722. 3 things we learned from the Bengals’ overtime win over the Titans

That's the second game in a row where the Cincinnati Bengals fell behind 13-0. Only this time, it came against a seemingly outmatched opponent, the Tennessee Titans.

This was one that Cincinnati easily could have lost, and that would have been a disaster in a tight AFC North.

Instead, it resulted in a thrilling overtime victory that taught us a lot about how the team (especially the defense) has grown.

Against the Baltimore Ravens two weeks ago, the Bengals got 35 points in the second half.

Then, against Tennessee, the Bengals scored zero points in the first quarter but ended up with 43.

Tee Higgins got the ball rolling, and Ja'Marr Chase led the way late. But the engine was, of course, Joe Burrow, who finished 38-of-48 for 462 yards, with five touchdowns, three interceptions, and a rushing touchdown.

To put that into perspective, Burrow became the first quarterback since 1951 to get 450 yards, five touchdowns, and a rushing touchdown in the same game. (The fact that the Bengals QB did something that got "Norm Van Brocklin" trending 43 years after his death is saying something.)

So when the defense did what it has done so often in recent years (give up long plays and turn borderline starting QBs into superstars), the offense didn't blink. Burrow and the Bengals just continued to fire downfield, not letting interceptions get in the way, because they know they can outlast anyone.

It's not just the 10 catches for 155 yards. It's the fact that Tee Higgins looks more dominant than he ever has before. He's manhandling defensive backs, catching in traffic, catching over the top of their heads, and not showboating afterwards.

He knows who he is: one of the very best in the game.

What's really noticeable is how easy it seems to be for him. Higgins doesn't even seem to be going full speed, but he's getting right by guys because of how confident he is in his route running, hands, and big body, which is always going to win.

Higgins now has totaled 148 yards or more in three of seven games. He's on pace for 104 catches, 1,763 yards, and 10 touchdowns, which has only been done six times before.

Forget the WR2 or WR1A talk. Just enjoy the fact that the Bengals have two supremely talented receivers, and neither of them can be contained for an entire game.

Burrow pointed out that this Titans game was precisely the kind of contest they'd lost the last three years.

And it looked bound to happen again, with Cam Ward driving to get near field goal range with under a minute left.

But then Dexter Lawrence got a monstrous sack, grabbing hold of Ward and slamming him to the ground.

It was the most dominant sack these eyes have seen since Geno Atkins propelled Deshaun Watson into the air back in 2017.

That play brought the Bengals back to life. And it was the kind of play that was missing, especially from the interior of the defensive line, for so many years.

It was the result of a beautiful collaboration with Boye Mafe. According to Paul Dehner Jr., "Lawrence and Mafe gave each other a look" and then we had "Mafe banging into Lawrence's blocker, helping free the 350-pound wrecking ball to slam Titans quarterback Cam Ward to the ground for a sack."

The two combined for another huge play in the third quarter, when Mafe strip-sacked Ward, and Lawrence picked up the ball and returned it eight yards (he was tragically tripped before he could take it all the way—that would have been an all-time highlight).

Those two plays, along with Demetrius Knight Jr. shooting through the gap to tackle Tony Pollard for a safety, showed you precisely the kind of game-changing plays that are possible when you're consistently winning in the trenches.

#2720. Avalanche sign star Cale Makar to largest contract in NHL history at $163.2 million

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

This has been the summer of spending in the NHL, and the Colorado Avalanche just broke the bank for star defenseman Cale Makar. On Friday, the team announced that Makar signed an eight-year extension worth $163.2 million.

The contract is the richest in league history -- both in total value and annual value at $20.4 million per year. Makar is the first player in NHL history to cross the $20 million salary threshold.

At 27-years old, Makar is arguably the best defensemen in the NHL, and he will remain in that conversation for quite a while. Makar has already won the Norris Trophy twice, and he was a key factor in Colorado's Stanley Cup run, which ended with him winning the Conn Smythe Trophy.

This past season, Makar posted monster numbers from the blue line yet again as he tallied 20 goals and 59 assists in 75 games. Since entering the NHL in 2019, Makar leads all defensemen in goals (20) and points (507).

"I am so excited and humbled to continue to wear the Avalanche sweater and represent this incredible organization and community," Makar said in a statement. "I would like to thank the Kroenke family, Joe Sakic and the entire Avalanche organization for their commitment, trust and belief in me. I would also like to thank my wife and family for their constant support, as well as Scott, Brian and Steve Bartlett for their guidance and assistance.

"To the Avalanche fans, thank you for your continued support and for welcoming us to Colorado years ago. Colorado has truly become a second home to us, and we are so grateful to be here. I look forward to getting back on the ice with my teammates and continuing to work toward our goal of bringing the Stanley Cup back to the Mile High City."

Over the last three seasons, Makar's impact has been immense in all three zones. He's posted a five-on-five expected goals share of 54.5%, per Natural Stat Trick. With Makar on the ice in those situations, Colorado has outscored its opponents 220-157. In two of the last three seasons, Makar has hit the 90-point mark, and he has 100-point potential at his best.

Makar's $11.4 million raise kicks in in at the start of the 2026-27 season, and it will make things significantly tighter for the Avalanche as they navigate the salary cap. The bright side for Colorado -- and the key in getting this deal done -- is that the team now has each of its core players signed through at least 2031.

There may be some sticker shock upon seeing the $20.4 million average annual value, but that's the new reality in the NHL as the cap rises exponentially. The previous record for highest salary in NHL history was just set earlier this offseason when the Anaheim Ducks signed center Leo Carlsson to a contract worth $18 million per year, and the Chicago Blackhawks announced a $75 million extension for Connor Bedard.

The next domino to fall will be an extension for Minnesota Wild defenseman Quinn Hughes, who is neck-and-neck with Makar as the best defensemen in the world. Waiting until after the Makar deal was announced to sign Hughes could prove to be a mistake for Wild general manager Bill Guerin.

#2719. Sixers backcourt singles out LeBron James for calming influence

PHILADELPHIA -- The Philadelphia 76ers are 6-1 following a win over the Charlotte Hornets on Saturday night. It was another win the Sixers were able to pull out in the final minutes despite trailing by double digits and not finding much offensive rhythm in the second half.

Even though LeBron James didn't play in that game due to it being the second night of a back-to-back, the Sixers were still able to take lessons they have learned thus far and apply them to this situation. James has seen literally every single scenario a basketball player can ever see in his lifetime. Therefore, he stays calm and ready in a lot of these moments, which then gets passed down to his younger teammates.

"Leadership," Tyrese Maxey stated of James. "Leadership. Calming presence. He's going to get a lot of rebounds, maybe go get the ball and calm us down. At the end of the day, it's LeBron James. He can do the stuff like he did tonight (Friday against the Knicks). He got a couple of big buckets."

James finished with 20 points, nine rebounds, and eight assists in Friday's win over New York and he kept the team calm and focused on the task at hand. A slow start means nothing in this league when there's so much talent up and down the roster and there is still so much time left on the clock. That's the message James continues to preach to the team and the group is listening.

"He kind of been in a bunch of different scenarios, he's been in the league 24 years, 25 years, he's seen a bunch of different end-of-game situations," added VJ Edgecombe. "So, he's composed, he's relaxed, he knows, but he's also just so vocal. That kind of helps us. That helps us all the time, just him being so vocal and, like I said, just gives us the confidence to guard, just expects certain actions or he calls out something before it happens type thing."

The fact that James and the Sixers have found ways to close out these types of games is an encouraging sign. Of course, Philadelphia would rather not have to play from behind so often, but this is a good step for this group as they continue to move forward.

"Yeah, it's going to be extremely encouraging," Maxey said. "I think we're going to be in a lot of close games, and, um, it's going to be big time for us to be in close games. We have been able to get stops defensively late in games."

#2716. 2026 NHL free agent tracker: Patrick Kane returns to Blackhawks on two-year contract

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

NHL free agency has slowed down in late July, but some notable names are still coming off the board. Most notably, Patrick Kane is returning to the Chicago Blackhawks on a two-year contract worth $16 million, the team announced on Thursday.

Already a Chicago legend and future Hall of Famer, Kane won three Stanley Cups and a slew of individual awards with the franchise that selected him with the No. 1 overall pick in 2007. Kane's first stint with the Blackhawks lasted 16 seasons, and he piled up 446 goals and 779 assists in 1,161 games. Kane ranks inside the top five of just about every statistical category in franchise history, and he will get the chance to keep climbing those lists over the next two years.

The Blackhawks sent Kane to the New York Rangers at the 2023 NHL trade deadline, and he played just 19 regular season games there before hitting free agency the next summer. Hip surgery delayed Kane's decision until November of that year, but he ultimately landed with the Detroit Red Wings, where he's spent the last three seasons.

Last season was Kane's best with Detroit, and it proved that he still had some gas left in the tank, at least offensively. Kane posted 16 goals and 41 assists in 67 games -- with 19 of those points coming on the power play.

In his second stint with the Blackhawks, Kane will add another level of playmaking to the power play, and he should strengthen a top six forward group that's bereft of proven talent. Kane will also be an excellent mentor and sounding board for fellow No. 1 overall pick, Connor Bedard, who is set to miss the first month of the season after undergoing shoulder surgery.

Kane isn't the player he once was, but he'll give Chicago a bit more pop at the top of the lineup, and his first game back in a Blackhawks jersey will be a huge night for the city.

#2713. Milwaukee Bucks vs. Minnesota Timberwolves Preview & Game Thread: Let’s get serious

The Milwaukee Bucks play their seventh game of the year tonight against the Minnesota Timberwolves, a squad widely seen as one of the Western Conference's best before the season began, but one that has had anything but a smooth start to the year, sitting just above .500. Of course, that bumpy ride is set to continue with the news that they will be without Anthony Edwards for about two months while he undergoes knee surgery. Although that news is obviously very bad for the Wolves—and you never wish injury on anyone—this opens the door for the Bucks in a game they otherwise would have had almost no shot at winning. These two teams played in the preseason, and the Wolves waxed the Bucks with little effort—hopefully that won't be repeated tonight.

The Timberwolves, after their offseason reshuffle, are still adjusting. After three scintillating opening wins from Minnesota—a 25-point win over Miami, a 22-point blowout over Orlando, and a 23-point win over Toronto—they fell flat in an overtime thriller against Cleveland, marked by turnover issues and late-game execution struggles. After the loss, news came out that Anthony Edwards would undergo knee surgery that would keep him off the court for up to two months.

Since Edwards has been out, the Timberwolves have gone 1-2, including a 121-111 loss to the San Antonio Spurs where new addition LaMelo Ball shot 2/10 and managed just 10 points in 20 minutes. Ball has had many exciting moments in Minny, but also some frustrating ones; his foul trouble and playmaking inconsistency have been issues at times. Crucially, Rudy Gobert has also started slow, and a lack of size outside Gobert—along with Donte DiVincenzo's absence—has contributed to an inconsistent seven games so far. Minnesota currently sits in 10th place in the West at 4-3, and they'll want to regain momentum heading into a stacked November.

Rudy Gobert has drawn online mockery after a rough start to the season. The 7'1" center has been in a shooting slump, going at just 41.2% from the field and sub-50% from the charity stripe; he even went 0/13 across a two-game stretch! Sure, Gobert has never been the most complete offensive player, but he's been flat-out inefficient on shots he usually makes, shooting just 48% on rim attempts. On the other hand, Gobert remains an elite rebounder (averaging north of 12 boards per contest) and one of the league's most intimidating defenders.

The matchup between Gobert and Myles Turner—another struggling center—will be very intriguing. Of course, the two have history, having got into an altercation in 2021 when Gobert played for the Jazz and Turner played for the Pacers. Keeping Gobert from finding an offensive rhythm and drawing him out of the key on defence will be crucial in the Bucks' attempt to secure their second win of the season.

Who: Milwaukee Bucks (1-5) vs. Minnesota Timberwolves (4-3).

Ousmane Dieng scores more than 10 points for the first time this season. He's gotten off to a slow start, averaging 2.4 PPG, 1.2 RPG, 1.2 APG on .422/.311/.716 shooting splits in just 11.8 minutes per night. However, this slump may be temporary, and despite Milwaukee's lockdown defense and standout wings, I sense a Dieng resurgence.

#2709. Game Preview #8: Wolves vs. Bucks Game Thread

On October 5th, the Minnesota Timberwolves played a preseason game against the Milwaukee Bucks in which the Wolves won by 19, behind a perfect 5/5 shooting night from Antonio Reeves, who is unfortunately no longer a member of the team.

Now, just under a month later, the Wolves will look to bounce back from a Halloween night loss to the San Antonio Spurs by looking to take out what is expected to be one of the worst teams in the East. Even if Minnesota is without Anthony Edwards and Rudy Gobert, they have more than enough talent to keep themselves above the 500 mark.

Let's get straight into some things to look out for, and some predictions, for Monday night's game.

Who: Minnesota Timberwolves (4-3) vs Milwaukee Bucks (1-5)

If you missed the Timberwolves Halloween hosing by the refs on October 31st, I don't blame you! You would've been better off enjoying some candy or horror movies – not my thing, but certainly someone's – than spending the evening watching as the officiating simply moved further and further in San Antonio's favor in a night in which LaMelo Ball fouled out.

However, to act like fouling hasn't been a concern for this Wolves team so far would be simply disingenuous and wrong.

Of all the Wolves' issues, from the injuries to the offensive inconsistency and the fit issues between Ball and Gobert, the biggest one fully in this team's control is the positions they put themselves in with the referees. Part of the blame can be on the zebras (in Ant's words), most of it must be on the players.

Especially on LaMelo Ball and Jaden McDaniels.

The Wolves have six different players (Ball, Gobert, Edwards, McDaniels, Ayo Dosunmu, Jonathan Kuminga) averaging over two fouls a game through only seven contests. While that pace will surely balance out as the season goes along, it's still quite a lot of fouls to be committing.

Beyond the 24 points-per-game in free throws those penalties could allow (not an exact science), foul trouble has kept many of the Wolves' most important players out of the game when the team needs help.

Even if the Bucks look like a bad team on paper, the Wolves aren't much better than them without two of their top three players and even more valuable pieces warming the bench because they antagonized the refs. Avoiding fouling will be paramount to getting back on track this season.

The Wolves have now played five games in seven days, including an overtime game against the Cleveland Cavaliers in the second game of that stretch.

Safe to say they are exhausted and in need of rest they are not going to get. Despite that, Minnesota is scheduled for this match against the Bucks just two days after their second back-to-back in five days. This is just a brutal set of games for any team to go through, and the Wolves being forced to do so without their two most floor-raising players means bad things for fans hoping for 50 wins.

Exhaustion is often underemphasized in the NBA. Stamina in games is properly accounted for, but stamina in seasons is not.

With how many star players have gotten hurt lately, maybe that's bound to change.

The NBA season is a marathon, not a sprint, but the Wolves have started their season with an obstacle course and ankle weights. To survive this stretch, maybe playing some deeper bench options in the hopes that they can simply eat innings, let alone help win games, could be a smart choice for head coach Chris Finch.

Either way, with only three games in the next weeklong span, the Wolves should slowly be able to catch their breath.

So far this season, Wolves fans have experienced the highs and lows of what LaMelo Ball can be.

To start the year, his fit with Anthony Edwards created gaudy scoring numbers and exciting highlights as the roster purred in sync, along with truly glorious crowd pops that only Target Center and maybe a handful of other arenas can produce.

However, over the past handful of games, LaMelo has been far less consistent and far more deserving of criticism. Last game, his fouling, although it was certainly exaggerated and embellished by the Spurs, left the Wolves without their offensive engine as San Antonio ran away with the win.

The highs have always been there for Ball. It's why he won Rookie of the Year over Ant in a year in which LaMelo was more exciting off the jump, while Edwards proved to be more consistent over a long season.

Stability, though, is what the Wolves need from him now. Without Ant present, Ball needs to be the offensive fulcrum he was for the Charlotte Hornets last year, in place of the organiser and maestro he's been to date in Minnesota.

Against the Bucks, who lack any particularly amazing defensive players, LaMelo should be dominating the ball and the opponents en route to a Wolves win.

If the Wolves do not win this game, I will be hiding in a bunker as Wolves Twitter proceeds to light the world on fire with takes about the recently benched Naz Reid and the worries of that 2033 first-round pick, which might not even matter if an asteroid hits the Earth or sports betting continues to burn at the fabric of league optics and fan interest.

Either way, Minnesota should take this one comfortably.

#2708. 2026-27 NHL season predictions: Expert picks for Stanley Cup playoffs, champion and major awards this season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Following a brief offseason and an expedited preseason, the 2026-27 NHL season has arrived. Before the puck drops on opening night, we have some predictions to make.

If this season feel like it's staring earlier than usual, that's because it is. The NHL is adopting an 84-game regular season, which just means more hockey for the rest of us. That also means a long and arduous journey to the Stanley Cup is ever so slightly more difficult.

So, what will that journey look like? The Carolina Hurricanes are looking to defend their title as Cup champions, but they'll have to contend with a deep Eastern Conference and some real juggernauts in the Western Conference. With that in mind, we logged our expert predictions for the playoff field in each conference -- and there were a few surprises -- before making our Stanley Cup Final selections.

We also called our shot on the winners of each major individual award. Connor McDavid is looking for his fourth Hart Trophy, but he's got some competition from an up-and-coming superstar in his own division. Races for the Norris Trophy and Vezina Trophy should be pretty wide open, and unexpected candidates always emerge throughout the season.

It should be a fun season in the NHL, so follow along with all our coverage at CBS Sports. Let's get things kicked off with the season preview and predictions, which will of course be 100% accurate.

Baumgartner: I don't see many new faces entering the conversation when it comes to the Eastern Conference playoff race. A healthy Florida Panthers side will slot themselves right back towards the top of the Atlantic, and a revamped Washington Capitals side should be able to make some noise in the Metropolitan. Besides that, I have six 2026 playoff teams returning to the dance in 2027.

Nivison: As much as I hate to go with chalk in preseason predictions -- because it rarely happens that way -- there's no denying the top dogs in the West. The Avalanche and Stars are the class of the Central Division, and the Golden Knights should pound a pitiful Pacific Division into a pulp. Things get more interesting behind those clear Cup contenders, and I'm projecting another significant leap forward from the Mammoth. I also think Macklin Celebrini will be successful in dragging the Sharks to the playoffs in his third NHL season.

Nivison -- Columbus Blue Jackets: The Blue Jackets have been agonizingly close to the playoffs in each of the last two seasons, and I think they get over the hump in 2026-27. There are still questions in Columbus. Can Adam Fantilli be a franchise player at center? Is the forward group as a whole good enough to keep pace in a competitive Eastern Conference? Still, I am sure the Blue Jackets have a really strong blue line, led by Norris Trophy winner Zach Werenski, and goaltender Jet Greaves is on track to become a Vezina Trophy candidate. Internal improvements from the young core will then get Columbus above the cut line.

Baumgartner -- San Jose Sharks: The Sharks narrowly missed out on the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, finishing just four points short of the second wild card. San Jose added a good group of veterans over the summer, but the most important offseason move was selecting Ivar Stenberg with the No. 2 pick in the Draft. Stenberg joins the youth movement in San Jose, which is spearheaded by new captain Macklin Celebrini, who broke the Sharks single-season points record with 115 last season. The Sharks are a better team than they were last year, and with Celebrini entering his third season as a legit Hart Trophy contender, this team won't be fun to play against.

Nivison: Yes, the Mammoth have a brutal path coming out of the Central Divison, but just close your eyes and imagine this scenario with me. Logan Cooley becomes a superstar center. Dylan Guenther hits 50 goals. Dmitry Simashev asserts himself as a budding top-four defenseman. Anders Lee and Vincent Trocheck provide necessary veteran depth. Now open your eyes. Utah is your Western Conference champion.

Unfortunately for the Mammoth, they will run into a refreshed Panthers team that now has double-barreled Tkachuks. Last season, we found out that all it takes to stop Florida is to hope all of its key players miss significant time with injury. The long offseason was probably a blessing in disguise as it allowed the Panthers to get healthy, and that's bad news for everyone else. The structure in front of the crease will limit some of the volatility we saw from Jacob Markstrom in New Jersey, and Florida wins its third Stanley Cup in four years.

Baumgartner: Before last season, the Carolina Hurricanes' kryptonite was the Eastern Conference Final. The Hurricanes were able to overcome their demons and win the East before ultimately taking home the franchise's first Stanley Cup since 2006. In the West, the Dallas Stars have been running into the same problem. After three straight seasons ending in the Western Conference Final, the Stars regressed last postseason, flaming out in the first-round to the Minnesota Wild. The Central Division will once again be a gauntlet, but I'm ready for Dallas to take the next step and reach the Stanley Cup Final.

While Dallas has continued to fall short in recent years, the Panthers have done the opposite. The Panthers made three consecutive Stanley Cup Final appearances, winning back-to-back Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. Last season, Florida's three-peat attempt came to a halt on day one of training after captain Aleksander Barkov went down with a non-contact injury, tearing both the ACL and MCL in his right knee. An offseason of healing for Barkov, and the rest of the banged up Panthers, has the team refreshed entering September for the first time in years. With nearly the entire 2025 Stanley Cup winning core still on the team and Brady Tkachuk added to the fold, Florida looks ready to win its third Stanley Cup in four seasons.

Nivison: Celebrini should have won the Hart Trophy last season, but for some incomprehensible reason, he wasn't even a finalist. This year, Celebrini replicates that performance and gets San Jose to the postseason to take home his first MVP award at age 20. Hughes posts a career year in his first full season with the Wild, and Spencer Carberry gets his flowers for winning the Metro Division after missing the playoffs last year.

Baumgartner: McDavid's ability to take over a game was evident nearly every time he touched the ice last season. His 24 points (11 goals,13 assists) in the final 14 games of the regular season -- without Leon Draisaitl in the lineup -- was one of the many reasons I put him No. 1 on my Hart Trophy ballot. With just two years left on his current contract, desperation may start to kick in to get the job in Edmonton, which would lead to another MVP-caliber season. Barkov is healthy and the frontrunner to win his fourth Selke, and Dahlin will have another strong season to take home his first career Norris Trophy.

On Friday, the Indianapolis Colts stole San Francisco 49ers defensive lineman Kevin Givens off their practice squad, and just two days later, another AFC South team had taken another.

According to KPRC2's Aaron Wilson, the Houston Texans are signing 49ers defensive lineman Naquan Jones off their practice squad.

Jones, 28, played at Michigan State from 2016-20, before going undrafted in 2021. He's bounced around the league quite a bit, with stints with the Tennessee Titans, Arizona Cardinals, Los Angeles Chargers and Houston Texans before joining the 49ers back in September.

In three games for San Francisco this season, Jones has recorded two tackles while playing 21% of their defensive snaps. Now, without him and Givens, the 49ers are left with Osa Odighizuwa, DeForest Buckner, Gracen Halton, Sebastian Valdez and James Thompson Jr. at the position on the 53-man roster. Their lone practice squad defensive lineman is McKinnley Jackson.

#2705. 2026-27 NBA News, Injury Updates Nov. 2: Injuries hit Jalen Williams, Cason Wallace, Chet Holmgren in OKC

Welcome to our weekly Monday Morning NBA notebook, a quick hit of NBA news and injuries from around the league to catch you up on the past seven days. My opinion on the first two weeks of this season? I stand with Jeff Stotts (of InStreetClothes.com).

This was simply as bad a week as a team can have.

Jalen Williams suffered a dislocated left ankle and fractured fibula from a fall last Sunday against the Clippers. "This is an injury that generally we see more in football players," Thunder general manager Sam Presti said. In that same game, starting guard Cason Wallace left with a shoulder injury that turned out to be a torn labrum in his left shoulder, which will also require surgery. While the Thunder will not put a timeline on either player, it's unlikely either of them plays again this season.

Later in the week, the Thunder announced that Chet Holmgren underwent a "biological treatment today to address a small patellar tendon tear" and will be out 8-10 weeks. That likely puts his return around New Year's or in the first couple of weeks of 2027. (If you're wondering what a "biological treatment" is, a league source suggested it's platelet-rich plasma, PRP, therapy.)

While Holmgren will return, the injuries to Williams and Wallace diminish their title chances. Oklahoma City will still be very good behind two-time MVP Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and a deep roster. However, they go from a playoff team that can beat anyone regardless of style to one that will be more matchup-dependent (how do they stop elite wings such as Anthony Edwards or Luka Doncic in the West without Williams or Lu Dort, whom they traded away this summer for financial reasons).

What you shouldn't expect is Presti and OKC to panic into a trade to "fix" things. That's not how Presti operates, and he's been in this job 19 years he's not at risk of getting fired. The Thunder will go forward, see what their team looks like, who is reasonably available, then make a call.

Minnesota's Anthony Edwards underwent arthroscopic surgery on his ailing right knee and that could sideline him up to two months. Which sucks, Edwards had played at an MVP level to start the season, averaging 33.3 points, 4.8 rebounds and 3.5 assists per game while shooting 40% from 3-point range.

The positive spin for Timberwolves fans is that this is a proactive move by Edwards and the team: Get the work done now, have him back and healthy around Christmas, or heading into 2027. Looking at the landscape of the West this is a team with sky-high expectations but it needs that MVP-level Edwards to get there.

In the short term, Minnesota needs more of the Charlotte version of LaMelo Ball: One who takes on a larger scoring load and lifts up teammates. So far, Minnesota is 1-2 since Edwards went out.

Portland — and how well the Ja Morant and Damian Lillard backcourt was clicking — was one of the early-season stories. This news just threw cold water on it.

Morant left his return to Memphis early and the next day came the news that he would be out at least a month with a strained hamstring. Expect Jrue Holiday to move into the starting five, but the real guy to watch is Scoot Henderson, who is going to get a real chance after starting the season coming off the bench and not looking sharp (7.5 points per game on 34.4% shooting)

Morant looked the best he has in years to start the season, averaging 16.3 points and 6.3 assists per game while shooting 58.8% overall and 44.4% from beyond the arc. He had a more mature game.

The timing of this sucks: Kawhi Leonard will miss his one game this season at the Intuit Dome in Los Angeles against the Clippers.

Leonard is out due to swelling in his left knee and will be re-evaluated later this week, the team announced last week. Toronto said in its release that Leonard "will undergo a treatment and rehabilitation program to address swelling in his left knee. Medical imaging revealed no acute injury." Leonard said this on social media.

The reality is the Raptors knew what they were signing up for when they traded for Leonard, that he would miss time and there would be load management. Expect Leonard to miss a couple of weeks as the Raptors will keep him in bubble wrap this season.

After missing so much of last season, it's been great to see Tyrese Haliburton back on the court — except now we won't see him for at least a couple of weeks due to a left hamstring strain.

This is trouble for the Pacers, who are getting outscored by 10.4 points per 100 possessions when Haliburton is off the court this season, and they are now 0-3 since he went out after falling to previously winless Brooklyn on Sunday.

It's been a rough start to the season in Utah and this just piles on top of it: Jaren Jackson Jr. is out with a torn MCL in his right knee. The good news is that it doesn't require surgery. Utah says Jackson Jr. will be reevaluated in six weeks but expect him to miss closer to eight weeks,

Utah was going to roll out a big front line this season with Jusuf Nurkic, Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen. Except we haven't seen it. Nurkic has yet to play due to a partial plantar plate tear in the second toe of his right foot, and now JJJ is out until Christmas or later.

Already without Paolo Banchero, more bad injury news for Orlando with the news guard Jalen Suggs is out with a right knee bone bruise and will be re-evaluated in two weeks. The good news is an MRI revealed no other structural damage.

Sean Sweeney, welcome to coaching Orlando.

• It's the end of an era. After 37 years, beloved host Ernie Johnson is stepping away from "Inside the NBA" after this season, he announced on X.

• We aren't done with the injury news: The Washington Wizards announced that forward Justin Champagnie underwent a surgical procedure to repair a fracture in his right foot, something he suffered during last week's game against Charlotte.

• Former NBA player Malik Beasley, who was indicted earlier this year for federal gambling crimes, will be changing his plea to guilty. Beasley was charged with manipulating his play in four games while he was with the Milwaukee Bucks during the 2023-24 season to help him pay off a loan after falling into debt

• Philadelphia applied for a disabled player exception due to Ariel Hukporti's season-ending Achilles tear. It's not much, it's just a $1.7 million exception (half of Hukporti's salary this season), but it's something they might use.

• Hall of Famer Paul Pierce is claiming he is "tapped out" financially in court documents in a case about support payments to an ex-girlfriend and the mother of one of his children.

#2703. Mainoo accepts fan frustration but is confident Man Utd can recover

Kobbie Mainoo is confident that Manchester United are "one win away" from changing the direction of their season and insists the players remain fully behind Michael Carrick.

United have endured a difficult campaign so far but Mainoo says the focus has to remain on the games ahead rather than their recent results.

"Of course, it's been a tough season. We've not had the results we've wanted," Mainoo said.

"But we need to look forward now. There's big, big games ahead and I feel like we're one win away from changing that."

Mainoo, who came through United's academy, also urged some perspective.

"I've been at this club for a long time and I know there's always going to be ups and downs," he said.

"It's never going to be plain sailing and smooth to the top so you expect bumps and the best thing about it is you're able to bounce back from them."

Mainoo also says the squad need to repay the support Carrick has shown the players.

"Yeah of course, I feel like our way to repay that is to also be behind the manager on the pitch and off it and fight for us and fight for us as a team," he continued.

"I'm very grateful to the boss for putting the trust in me as soon as he came in and putting that belief in me.

"And giving me all the advice that he has, knowing that he's been a player for this club and knows the history of this club and what it takes to win.

"I take those words to heart and try to apply them every day in training and in games."

#2700. Is Cooper Flagg already a top-10 player?

Is Cooper Flagg already a top-10 player at just 19 years old?

This season we've watched Flagg lead Dallas to wins while outplaying Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Giannis Antetokounmpo, and he handed Houston its first loss behind a 33-point, 9-rebound, 6-assist effort.

In the final 100 seconds on Friday, he made two back-breaking shots that led the Mavericks to an NBA Cup victory:

First, Flagg drained an and-one floater that put Dallas up five points, and later he drove right and spun left into a heavily contested fallaway.

The floater is becoming a bit of a signature shot for Coop. Consider these three moments against Oklahoma City:

Here, the Mavericks run Flagg through a double screen on the left side of the floor, then he drives but is met at the rim by 7-foot-3 rookie center Aday Mara. So Flagg elevates and tosses up a soft floater.

Later on, Flagg brings the ball up himself and once again sees Mara inside so he tosses it up for another bucket.

The next play up the floor, Dallas runs a high pick-and-roll for Flagg with Daniel Gafford screening. Mara sees Flagg coming so he rotates over and contests hard. But that's not a floater — that's a lob to Gafford. The mere threat of a floater creates openings for his teammates, which puts the defensive big man in a dilemma: step up to stop the floater, and the same motion becomes a lob.

Flagg always had the floater in his bag. This year he's just making it more of a threat and he's improved his midrange pull-up. At Duke, Flagg made only 34% of his dribble jumpers from midrange. As a rookie in Dallas, he made 38%. So far this season, he's made 76%. That number is obviously unsustainable, but we'll see where it lands; Flagg has always had excellent touch as an 83% career free-throw shooter. The ability to make late-clock jumpers off the dribble at an efficient clip is the weapon that often separates All-NBA players from All-Stars, and right now Flagg has it.

Flagg still needs to grow in the 3-point department. He made 28% of his catch-and-shoot 3s and 30% of his dribble-jumper 3s as a rookie. Those numbers are pretty comparable so far in his second year. But given his month-to-month rate of improvement, it may only be a matter of time until the 3 is a knockdown shot for him. Maybe it'll even happen by the end of season.

Flagg is complementing that offensive growth with defense that is swinging games.

At 6-foot-10, Flagg is a Swiss Army knife who can defend across positions. You'll see him defend guards, and slide his feet to contain drives, he'll match up against big wings like Kevin Durant, and his coaching staff can feel comfortable with him battling against a true big.

Among the 100 players who have defended the most isolations since Flagg entered the NBA, Flagg ranks 13th in points allowed per play — one spot behind Stephon Castle and two spots behind Chet Holmgren, to put into perspective the company he's among.

Up 33 on the Pacers and defending Aaron Nesmith, Flagg attempts to steal the ball on the entry to Pascal Siakam before rotating right back over to steal it on the return. This starts a transition basket that ends with Nesmith clearly being a bit frustrated with a hard foul on Flagg that fortunately caused him to miss just a game.

And as good as Flagg is on the ball, he's an even better instinctive and disruptive help defender with quick reflexes to alter shots and swipe at the ball.

Flagg's best two-way sequence of the year came in the clutch against Miami:

With Dallas protecting a two-point lead, Miami pushes the ball up the floor and finds Andrew Wiggins seemingly open in the corner, but Flagg closes out hard, extends his right hand, and gets a fingertip on the shot to cause the airball. Flagg has always hustled like a madman on the floor, but he's also got great athleticism and instincts to actually make plays like this one.

Back up on the other end, Flagg crosses over to create space, drives hard, and gets his body by Wiggins before gathering the ball toward the rim as help arrives from 1-2-3 defenders. But look at his left-handed extension to evade them and preserve a finishing angle through the contest, turning a one-possession game into a four-point lead with 10 seconds left.

The ability to do this in traffic speaks to Flagg's dexterity, coordination, and improvements as a ball-handler. At lower levels, Flagg could always plow through defenders with hard straight-line drives. He has a freight-train finishing ability. But he didn't have great creativity off the bounce and he's progressed there to now use some wiggle and spin moves to get where he wants. On the year, he's making 69% of his layups, which is up from 52% as a rookie.

New Mavericks head coach Dusty May is designing actions to slingshot Flagg toward the basket. Sometimes to score on his own with gliding layups. Other times for kick-out passes to open shooters to take advantage of collapsing defenses. On some occasions, the player on the receiving end has been Kyrie Irving.

Flagg's chemistry is already blossoming with Kyrie. If Flagg is on the ball, Irving provides him an elite catch-and-shoot guy from 3 to target. Or Kyrie can set an inverted screen for him, something we saw Kyrie do for years to great effect alongside LeBron James.

But Irving can also run the show while Flagg moves around off-ball. Flagg has the ability to operate as both a play creator and a play finisher. As great as he's been on-ball this year, he can also set screens, cut with purpose, spot up, and crash the glass. So it's not a huge surprise that he's vibing with Kyrie, a similarly selfless player who can score or playmake. That willingness to give the ball up is part of the reason the Flagg leap is happening this year too.

I've scouted Flagg since he was in high school. The fact he is already this good at just 19 is kind of shocking, to be honest. He wasn't supposed to be doing these things this soon. But it follows a trend. He got way better after turning 18 years old at Duke. Then over the final 26 games of his rookie season, he averaged 25 points, 7 rebounds, and 5 assists. His surge was highlighted by a 51-point performance that helped him win Rookie of the Year. And so far this year, he's averaging 27/6/7 on elite scoring efficiency, an even better assist-to-turnover ratio and more impactful defense.

What's this production gonna look like by the end of the season when so far he's clearly been one of the league's five-to-10 best players? People will say I am being reactionary, but again: What we're seeing from Flagg right now follows a natural trajectory. It's not like this is me saying Ty Jerome is a top-10 guy because of some out-of-nowhere unstoppable performances. Flagg has been on this path for multiple years now.

So whether you want to say he's a top-five guy, a top-10 guy, or not even top 20 yet because you want to give him more time, what's happening is undeniable. Cooper Flagg has arrived.

#2699. Detroit Lions grades, report card: The run game finally arrives vs. Vikings

Let's hand out some grades for the Detroit Lions' gritty 19-15 win over the Minnesota Vikings.

Jared Goff's final statline isn't all that impressive, but he commanded the offense to a relatively successful day. After shaking off a first half of four sacks, Goff successfully avoided negative plays against this harrowing defense. Obviously, the interception wasn't on him. You could argue he held onto the ball a little too long in the first half, but the Vikings' coverage was often very good on those plays.

Ultimately, I was impressed by Goff's ability to stay calm and disciplined despite the tough start. We've seen him—and just about every NFL quarterback—get rattled by this defense before, but Goff kept his head, found the open receivers in the second half (7-of-9 for 66 yards, 1 TD) and even threw his body around a little in the run game.

Per NextGenStats, Jahmyr Gibbs forced 12 missed tackles on his 25 touches on his way to a 153-yard rushing day. But it was Sione Vaki who got a ton of attention for his breakout performance. His 11 carries for 65 yards may not seem like much, but it felt like he was the key to opening up the run game against the Vikings. His downhill running style led to an impressive 45% success rate on runs (Gibbs was 42%).

As a team, Detroit produced 10 rushes of 10+ yards against the Vikings—who had given up just 14 for the entire season prior to this game. And a lot of that had to do with the backs' performances:

Early in the game, it felt like the Lions' tight ends were largely responsible for some protection busts. Sam LaPorta and Tyler Conklin looked directly responsible for one sack each in the first half.

However, this unit rebounded in a huge way in the second half. Having one or two tight ends in the backfield really seemed to neutralize the Vikings pass rush, and it opened up some massive rushing lanes, as well. Just look how impactful it was to have some sort of skill position player in the backfield (most often a tight end):

Jameson Williams now has five touchdowns in his last three games, as he continues to be a weapon at every point on the field. Amon-Ra St. Brown's statline is modest (seven catches, 46 yards), but that was on eight targets. His impact was still felt in key moments.

Both players were tagged with taunting penalties, and there were times it didn't feel like they were getting open quick enough. And Williams' untimely slip on his route not only cost Detroit an opportunity to convert a third down but led to Goff's only interception on the year.

It was far from a bad day from the receivers, but we know they can play better than this.

It felt like some of the early pressures weren't on the Lions offensive line, although there were certainly some missed assignments and lost one-on-ones in the run game early.

However, everything cleared up in the second half. Despite facing a blitz on 26-of-29 dropbacks (89.7%), the Lions offense allowed a pressure rate of just 24.1%—the third-lowest of any team in Week 8 and Minnesota's lowest pressure rate of the season. The Vikings' previous low was 41.3%.

I've already gone through a lot of the impressive rushing stats, but here's a few more. The Lions had the sixth best rushing success rate (47.4%) of the week, which was also the highest mark the Vikings have allowed all season.

Detroit's rushing game has been decent all year, but this was the first time it looked like where it was at during its peak days under Ben Johnson.

According to PFF, the Lions produced just 12 pressures and NFL Pro had them at a 33.3% pressure rate (14th of the week) with an average time of 3.26 to pressure (third slowest of Week 8). They were fine against the run, but Detroit's pass rush has slowly been fading a bit over recent weeks. Thankfully, the Lions dialed up a few successful blitzes in this game, and in the rare occasions Kyler Murray was able to escape the pocket, he didn't do much damage.

The interior of the defensive line continues to carry the load. Alim McNeill and Skyler Gill-Howard both had a sack, while Tyleik Williams is a force in the run game and drew a holding penalty.

The Lions found a little spark with Jimmy Rolder, who had a sack and a tackle for loss on the game. And coverage didn't seem to be as big of an issue this week as in previous weeks. While T.J. Hockenson was a bit of a problem, the Lions mostly used defensive backs on him.

We need to talk about the rebound D.J. Reed is currently going through. He had three pass breakups in this game, and PFF credited him with just a single catch allowed on five targets for 11 yards and an interception. Since Week 5, Reed is the No. 1 graded cornerback by PFF (90.7) with the best coverage grade (91.0).

Unfortunately, the rest of the secondary was very up and down. Granted, they often forced Murray to hold the ball long, they still gave up too many big plays and there are still too many coverage busts.

Roger McCreary missed a key tackle on Aaron Jones that immediately led to a touchdown. Brian Branch, Chuck Clark, and Christian Izien all had issues on the back end.

Obviously, the mistakes didn't hurt them too much against a Vikings pass attack that just can't find its identity, but against a better team, Detroit will need to be much cleaner on the back end.

Detroit's coverage units were fantastic against one of the biggest return threats in the NFL. Myles Price managed just 24.0 yards per kick return, well below his 29.7 average. He also didn't gain a single yard on his one punt return.

Jake Bates was okay. He had two touchbacks on kickoffs, although I'm certain the last one was intentional, and his missed his first field goal of the year. But Jack Fox picked up the mantle, putting three of his four punts inside the 20-yard line.

There were some in-game decisions I didn't approve of much. At the end of the first half, I think the Lions bled too much clock. Dan Campbell likes to make sure they have the final possession in each half, but when you're going up against a bad Vikings offense, I think the priority needs to be maximizing your own points rather than being fearful of giving Kyler Murray too much time.

I also believe Campbell was wrong to go for a two-point conversion with five minutes still left in the third quarter. Considering the Vikings notoriously score field goals and not touchdowns, being up six rather than five is a pretty significant difference. I don't think there was enough motivation to try to be up by seven with that much time left.

But, a ton of credit goes to offensive coordinator Drew Petzing for a game plan that found actual, real solutions to Brian Flores' defense. The tight ends in the backfield gave Detroit a numbers advantage in both the run and pass game. Some of the toss action caught the Vikings off kilter, like on Detroit's 30-yard rushing touchdown.

Plus, Petzing went into his bag with that crazy St. Brown catch/lateral that converted a key third-and-8.

And on the other side, Kelvin Sheppard's unit has now produced three strong gameplans in a row, and against the Vikings, he had to deal with several key starters leaving the game. It should also not be lost on how the Lions kept their composure despite the Jack Campbell situation unfolding in the fourth quarter. That both a testament to the players and coaches on that sideline.

Grêmio and Palmeiras beat Atlético-MG and Vasco, respectively, in the first legs of the 2026 Copa do Brasil semifinalsCredits: LUCAS UEBEL/GREMIO FBPA and Cesar Greco/Palmeiras

Grêmio and Palmeiras took the advantage in the first legs of the Copa do Brasil semifinals on Sunday (1). At their arena in Porto Alegre, Grêmio beat Atlético-MG 2–0, with goals from Carlos Vinicius and Erick Noriega. Palmeiras, meanwhile, defeated Vasco 1–0 at Nubank Parque in São Paulo. #2697. Leipzig back into Champions League spot with dominant win over Schalke

FC Schalke 04 (1-3-3, 16th) played host to RB Leipzig (4-0-3, 6th) in the eighth matchweek of the 2026/27 Bundesliga season on Saturday afternoon.

Miron Muslić’s Königsblauen went into this match desperate for a victory to avoid the relegation zone, ahead of only 1. FC Union Berlin and Borussia Mönchengladbach in the table. In the last four matches for the Nordrhein-Westfalen side, they have picked up just two points (0-2-2), scoring one goal and conceding three. The Bundesliga has become their main focus, after their DFB-Pokal campaign ended in the second round to SG Dynamo Dresden by an 0-2 result this past Wednesday.

As for Martín Demichelis’ Roten Bullen, they have had relatively shaky results in recent weeks, with a 6-0 victory over Eintracht Frankfurt, a 1-6 defeat to FC Bayern München, and a 4-0 victory over SV Elversberg 07. This, combined with their current UEFA Champions League and DFB-Pokal campaigns, have caused a heavy schedule with consistent midweek matches for the Sachsen side - nearly leading to an elimination from the latter tournament before Christoph Baumgartner rescued his side to a 2-1 win over 3. Liga side Rot-Weiss Essen.

The two sides have met twelve times since Leipzig, founded in 2009, promoted to the Bundesliga for the first time in the 2016/17 season. Leipzig are 8-2-2 overall, and have won all of their last five meetings - outscoring Schalke by a 22-3 margin in that span. In the 2023/24 season, the most recent for Schalke in the German top-flight, Leipzig won 6-1 away and 4-2 at home; the last time Schalke won in Leipzig was on 28. September 2019 (3-1), and their last home win against Leipzig was on 19. August 2017 (2-0).

The match kicked off with Schalke, in blue, going left to right, and Leipzig, in red, right to left. The hosts started the match with a 3-3-2-2 formation, but Muslić changed it to a 4-2-3-1 after just one minute - in an attempt to counter the 4-5-1 that Demichelis had prepared.

Leipzig won a free kick after just two minutes, thanks to Brajan Gruda as he was taken down by Hwang Hee-chan. David Raum delivered the free kick far-post, into the right side of the box; Willi Orbán was there and knocked it towards Timo Becker - who accidentally deflected the ball past Loris Karius and into his own net. Assistant official Sascha Thielert raised the flag for offside on the Hungarian international, however - and thus, head official Dr. Max Burda cancelled it.

Schalke would go the other way in the ninth minute, deflecting the ball off Neil El Aynaoui and out for a corner; the following delivery from Adil Aouchiche was blocked, but the ball fell at the feet of Satoshi Tanaka, who dropped it off to Mertcan Ayhan. The 20-year-old hometown talent delivered the ball back into the box, eventually finding an unmarked Junior Adamu - but the header from the Nigeria-born Austria international was not powerful enough and went into the arms of Maarten Vandevoort.

Adamu drew a free kick just four minutes later, pushed to the ground by Rocco Reitz. Aouchiche attempted to curl the ball above Vandevoort on the ensuing set piece, but smashed it off the bar and out. From there, Leipzig quickly went the other way - with an initial chance from Antonio Nusa denied by Karius, and a subsequent header from an unmarked Rômulo going just over the woodwork.

Nine minutes from halftime, Leipzig made their way into the right side of the Schalke penalty area, with Rômulo in possession. Tanaka attempted a sweeping tackle from behind to knock the ball away - but swept the legs of the Brazilian in the process, causing Burda to point to the spot. Karius guessed the side correctly, but his jump was a bit too late, as Nusa powered the ball towards the bottom-left corner with his right boot to open the scoring for the visitors.

Leipzig managed a second just before halftime, but like the Becker own goal that was disallowed, this one also came back quite quickly. The play started with a cross from Raum into the right side of the box from the left side of the Schalke third. The ball landed at the feet of Gruda, whose powerful shot was denied by Karius; the rebound was then tapped in by Rômulo, but Burda cancelled the goal out soon after because the ball went out of play at the moment of Raum’s delivery.

Shots in the opening half finished 7-4 to Leipzig, 3-1 on target with 60 % possession; both sides managed a pass accuracy of 85 %, but Leipzig managed 237 completions and Schalke 185. Touches in the opposing penalty area finished 23-5 to the visitors.

Rômulo attempted to get his goal back on the first chance of the second half, taking the ball from Adamu at the edge of the box and powering a shot past a diving Karius, just wide of the bottom-left corner. Five minutes later, Leipzig connected a series of quick passes on the left side of the Schalke half, with Nusa playing the ball into the left side of the box; Ezechiel Banzuzi was in open space to meet the ground pass, but Karius charged out of his goal and knocked the ball away from the 21-year-old DR Congo international for an eventually unsuccessful corner to the visitors.

For much of the first twenty minutes of the term, Schalke struggled to connect strong passes, taking and then quickly losing possession of the ball. However, in the sixty-third minute, they would see their first chance of the term. Hwang Hee-chan played the ball into the left side of the visiting third to Aouchiche; Henrichs stepped in front just in time to knock it away for a corner. The 24-year-old Algerian international crossed the ball into the centre of the box, aiming far-post, but Vandevoort read the play well and grabbed on with both hands to halt the hosts’ momentum.

There was no significant chance of note for another fourteen minutes; Demichelis made a couple of changes, one of them being the entry of Ridle Baku in place of Benjamin Henrichs in the seventy-sixth minute. Two minutes later, the German right-back began a dangerous counterattack into the right side of the Schalke half. His long ground pass got to Nusa, who then flicked the ball short to his left for Rômulo. Within a fraction of a second, the Brazilian sent the ball past a helpless Karius and into the bottom-right corner to secure a certain victory for the Red Bulls.

Schalke were held off target for the entirety of the second half, and Burda eventually called time on a 2-0 Leipzig victory. With the result, Leipzig moved back up into a UEFA Champions League spot, currently fourth; Schalke, on the other hand, remain in sixteenth, with 1. FC Union Berlin to potentially drop them into the relegation zone with a win or draw against 1. FC Köln tomorrow.

Leipzig held 61 % possession in the second half, while also outshooting Schalke 10-2, 6-0 on target. The visitors managed 17 touches in the opposing penalty area, compared to just 5; and pass accuracy was 87 % to Leipzig on 243 completions, compared to 80 % on 142 for Schalke. Overall, Leipzig outshot Schalke 17-6, 9-1 on target with 60 % possession, and a pass accuracy of 86 % on 480 completions to 83 % on 300. Touches in the opposing penalty area finished 43-10 in favour of the visitors.

RB Leipzig will play both of their next two matches at Red Bull Arena; they face Manchester City FC in the UEFA Champions League on Wednesday, 21.00 (CET), before taking on FC Augsburg next Saturday at 15.30 (CET). As for FC Schalke 04, they will visit Baden-Württemberg and PreZero Arena to take on TSG 1899 Hoffenheim next Sunday, with kickoff set for 19.30 (CET).

#2695. Breaking down Karl-Anthony Towns strong start to Knicks season — and what he can still improve

If there are any questions about the Knicks' commitment post-championship, or their distraction level amid contract negotiations, none of them can be pointed at Karl-Anthony Towns.

Coming off a legendary postseason run that helped secure his place in New York immortality, Towns has been his team's most locked-in player of the new season, averaging 21.8 points, 13.5 rebounds, and 3.2 assists per game on 65.5 percent shooting from two and 41.4 percent from three.

This, despite being the key hang-up in the Knicks' extension talks and coming off a busy summer of celebration. Let's dive into Towns' hellacious start and what it means to the team.

One difference from Towns this season is his frame. He came into the season considerably thinner than in years past, though he plans to bulk up as the year progresses.

This seems to only have benefited Towns' game. His mobility looks better and there haven't been major sacrifices on the defensive end or boards.

His inside finishing has been particularly efficient, while that was a weakness early last season.

Otherwise, it's been a lot of the Towns we know and love, specifically out of the hub offense that turned around last season's playoffs. The Knicks are leaning into it more now having the blueprint, and Towns looks as comfortable as ever with head coach Mike Brown's schemes.

It hasn't shown up on the stat sheet as many would have liked — Towns' turnovers have spiked while his assists are flat. But much of this is due to how teams have adjusted against this look.

They've been more aggressive in switching the flex screen and helping off the weak side, forcing the Knicks into the third and fourth option on these plays. There's also some sloppiness on Towns' part as he gets reacquainted and sees what passes he can force or not.

But these bumps are to be expected, the net is positive, and even some early hiccups are ultimately helpful toward the ultimate goal. The fact that the Knicks haven't made shots like normal is also skewing the numbers.

Inside or out of the hub offense, Towns has looked the part. His 41.4 percent three-point shooting mark could come on higher volume, but he's picked his spots well with deep catch-and-shoots off trails and even some self-creation in the clutch.

Towns has seen the most action in fourth quarters, scoring 7.3 of his points per game in that period. Unfortunately the Knicks haven't turned to him in the closing moments enough, as he's taken two shots in the eight minutes of crunch time in games New York's played thus far.

That the Knicks have lost most of these tight contests to fall to 2-4 record could be in part due to this. Until others pick up their slack, this may need to be more of a Towns-centric team.

Fans know first hand how these Towns reps will ultimately pay off in the playoffs, when the Knicks will need multiple answers and know they can depend on their big man. But they'll also play a role in the coming contract negotiations.

Towns can either hit free agency or re-sign long-term with the Knicks, with both parties seemingly favoring the latter -- just at different prices. He will have much more leverage walking in with continued dominance like this.

Towns can point to New York's falling point differential when he steps off the court, or the mixed results they're getting from their alternative second options on the wing. He can point to being second in the league in rebounds per game and first to the rim to defend it.

Hopefully this ends in an inked extension and repeat run. In the meantime, Towns is aiming to put together one of the best seasons of his career, and the early returns are promising.

#2694. Chiefs Week 8 snap count analysis: Cyrus Allen sees season-high workload

Welcome to Arrowhead Pride's weekly snap-count analysis!

Let's take a closer look at the Kansas City Chiefs' snap counts in the 28-24 loss to the Denver Broncos in Week 8. The starting lineups are courtesy of NFL Game Stats and Information, and the snap-count data comes from Pro Football Focus' premium stats.

Starters (offensive): LT Kahlil Benson, LG Mike Caliendo, C Creed Humphrey, RG Trey Smith, RT Jaylon Moore, QB Patrick Mahomes, WR Rashee Rice, WR Xavier Worthy, RB Kenneth Walker, TE Travis Kelce and TE Noah Gray

Starters (defensive): DE George Karlaftis, DT Chris Jones, DT Khyiris Tonga, DE Felix Anudike-Uzomah, LB Nick Bolton, LB Drue Tranquill, LB Jack Cochrane, CB Kristian Fulton, CB Nohl Williams, S Alohi Gilman and S Chamarri Conner

Did not play: QB Justin Fields, OT Joshua Ezeudu

Inactive: QB Garrett Nussmeier (Emergency third QB), CB Mansoor Delane (Shoulder), FB Ben VanSumeren, DE Jack Pyburn, DE Tyreke Smith and OT Diego Pounds

In Denver, wide receiver Xavier Worthy led all skill-position players in snaps (64) by playing 94% of the time the unit was on the field. It felt like wideout Rashee Rice (38 snaps, 56% of the offensive snaps), in his return from the hamstring tweak, was playing on a pitch count due to the soft-tissue injury

Rookie wide receiver Cyrus Allens stepped up to play 30 snaps, including 22 reps on pass plays. He out-snapped second-year wideouts Jalen Royals and Andrew Armstrong by 8 snaps, although those two saw more action in run-blocking situations.

Allen caught two passes on three targets, but the miss was nearly a huge play downfield; it appeared Allen wasn't anticipating the ball in tight coverage, so he slowed down on his route. He may not have been as open as it appeared due to that hesitation, but he still could've had a chance at a tight-window completion, a similar play as the ones he made in training camp to originally start the hype train.

Allen's 20 yards over the two catches were more than Worthy (13 yards) produced in less than half the playing time.

Lead back Ken Walker played 55 snaps and dominated the run share, but rookie Emmett Johnson had his breakout game despite just 13 offensive snaps. He saw just one handoff, but gained 15 yards on the tackle-breaking, highlight-reel play.

Johnson saw 12 snaps on pass plays and ran routes on 11 of those snaps (staying in for pass protection just once). He caught all five of the passes thrown his way and totaled 128 yards, including the 73-yard touchdown catch-and-run in the first half.

With 143 yards from scrimmage, Johnson out-produced Walker (84 yards) in 1/4 of the playing time. He also played nine snaps on special teams and gained 44 yards on his only kickoff return of the afternoon. With return specialist Nikko Remigio struggling, Johnson should be strongly considered as the primary returner moving forward.

The primary slot defender moving forward is Chris Roland-Wallace, and that seemed to be the case even before L'Jarius Sneed was placed on the Reserve/Injured list on Saturday. Roland-Wallace played 49 snaps in Denver and dominated the slot snaps.

However, rookie cornerback Jadon Canady was active for the second time this season and made an impact for the first time on defense. As the sixth defensive back in the Chiefs' Dime defense, a pass-down package predicated on coverage, Canady took seven snaps and made two tackles on third downs that were short of the sticks.

He only defended pass plays; he may not be ready to man the slot on neutral downs and defend the run, but he looks like an asset for the Chiefs' coverage moving forward.

#2689. The Washington Nationals will have plenty of roster decisions to make today

The MLB offseason is officially here, and November 2nd is one of the first big days on the calendar. Due to how the rules work, we could see a lot of minor moves today, and we know how much Paul Toboni loves that. Players are not allowed to be stashed on the 60-day IL for the offseason, so all 40-man rosters actually have to be cut to 40 today by 5 PM.

For the Nats, that means moves will have to be made. Right now, there are five players on the 60-day IL who either need to be DFA'd or re-added to the 40-man. Those players are Mitchell Parker, PJ Poulin, Ken Waldichuk, Matt Waldron and Drew Millas. Several of those guys are likely to be DFA'd, but we won't know for sure until later in the day.

The Nats are not the only team dealing with this situation. In San Francisco, Buster Posey has a busy day on his hands. As of October 29th, the Giants had 56 players on their 40-man roster. They had a lot of players go on the 60-day IL, but now they will have to trim that roster back down.

Paul Toboni is clearly monitoring that situation. In fact, he has already acquired two players from the Giants. First, he claimed RHP Braxton Roxby off waivers a few days ago. Then, he made a minor trade for second baseman Nate Furman, a speedy, contact oriented infielder. In that deal, the Nats gave up Tony Neubeck, who was an undrafted free agent in 2026. To clear space on the 40-man roster, the Nats DFA'd Richard Lovelady.

I could see Toboni and Ani Kilambi making more moves like this in the coming hours. They clearly like to churn through the back end of the 40-man roster in an attempt to find hidden gems. The results have been mixed so far, but Curtis Mead was a notable success story. There are going to be a lot of players DFA'd today, and I think the Nats will be keeping a close eye on the waiver wire.

The next month should be a hectic one across the league. Unless a deal is miraculously made, the CBA will expire in a month. Once that happens, teams will not be allowed to make any moves. That could mean we see a lot of blockbuster moves made in November. I also think we will see a ton of smaller moves as well. Executives will want as optimal of a 40-man roster as possible.

There are a number of key dates that are coming up. The GM and owner meetings are in the next couple of weeks. After that, the non-tender deadline is on November 20th. Paul Toboni is going to have quite a busy month.

Overall, this will be a busy day around the league. However, I think the Nats will be one of the busier teams. We could see a couple surprise DFA's or some minor deals like the Furman one. This new regime loves optimizing the back of the 40-man roster, so today probably feels like a holiday for Paul Toboni, Ani Kilambi and the rest of the front office. Let's see what goes down in the coming hours.

Jackson's injury, which came in the first quarter of Monday's loss to the Memphis Grizzlies when Ty Jerome fell into his knee, will not require surgery, according to ESPN.

That wasn't the only front-court injury Utah sustained in the loss, as Lauri Markkanen injured his wrist attempting to get around a screen in the first quarter. The team said Tuesday that Markkanen is considered day-to-day. Neither returned to the game as they played just 16 combined minutes in the defeat.

Even if Markkanen avoids serious injury, Jackson's absence puts the Jazz in an enormously difficult situation, considering the direction their offseason took. After a contract standoff with former starting center Walker Kessler, the Jazz elected to sign-and-trade him to the Los Angeles Lakers for two first-round picks and two first-round swaps. It's early, but Kessler has been spectacular for the Lakers, and his absence left the Jazz without a long-term option at center. Short-term starter Jusuf Nurkić is also injured, and now, the Jazz are without Jackson, their rim-protecting power forward.

Utah has spent the bulk of the past four seasons tanking. This season carried at least Play-In expectations after the emergence of Keyonte George last year and with the arrival of No. 2 overall pick Darryn Peterson. Those goals are obviously not out of reach even with Jackson injured, but a 1-3 start coupled with everything they've lost in the front-court certainly leaves Utah behind the eight ball early on. The Jazz already rank No. 25 in the NBA defensively, and while their rebounding has surprised early in the season, it is a clear weakness on paper.

The Jazz have the ammunition to make a sizable trade if they want to. That was one of the benefits of trading Kessler. But teams are rarely eager to give away valuable veterans early in seasons, and roughly 29% of all NBA players are not currently eligible for trades because of contracts they signed during the offseason.

For now, Utah will probably have to rely on incumbent big men like Jaxson Hayes, Mo Bamba and Kyle Filipowski while they await the return of at least Nurkić and then, eventually, Jackson.

#2687. Alexander Ovechkin announces this will be his last NHL season: 'Let's have fun'
