Alex Ovechkin's 22nd NHL season will be his last, the Washington Capitals superstar announced on Monday."This is gonna be my last year," Ovechkin told his teammates in a video the Capitals posted to social media. "It's sad, but it is what it is. We have an unbelievable team this year. There are 82 games left. Let's make the playoffs, and let's have fun."

Ovechkin has already established himself as the greatest goal-scorer in hockey history with 929 tallies, and he still has 82 games to add to that total before he hangs up his skates.

The No. 1 overall pick in the 2004 NHL Draft, Ovechkin immediately established himself as a prolific scorer by notching 52 goals en route to winning the Calder Trophy as a rookie.

Since then, Ovechkin has won the Rocket Richard Trophy as the NHL's leading goal-scorer a record nine times. The Capitals legend's resume also features an Art Ross Trophy and three Hart Trophy wins.

The crowning achievement in Ovechkin's illustrious career is leading Washington to its first Stanley Cup in 2017-18. After coming up short in a number of postseasons prior to that, Ovechkin led all playoff performers with 15 goals and won the Conn Smythe Trophy as a result.

Following the 2025-26 season, there was speculation that Ovechkin could retire, but he signed an incentive-laden one-year deal with the Caps.Sensing that this could be Ovechkin's final season, the Capitals loaded up to give their franchise icon one more shot at the Stanley Cup. Washington signed former Buffalo Sabres winger Alex Tuch in free agency and acquired winger Jordan Kyrou from the St. Louis Blues via trade.

No team is as loaded on the wings as the Capitals, and they have one of the best rosters in the Metro Division. Washington has the ingredients to challenge the defending Cup champion Carolina Hurricanes and get Ovechkin one more ring before he rides off into the sunset.

#2686. This Can’t Continue (But It Probably Will)

On Sunday afternoon at Ford Field, the Minnesota Vikings finally ran into a situation where their defense couldn't overcome what is becoming one of the worst offenses in recent team history.

The Vikings' offense had ten possessions on Sunday afternoon in Detroit (excluding their kneel down at the end of the first half). Only two of those possessions lasted longer than three minutes. The Lions had a more than eleven-minute advantage in time of possession (35:43 to 24:17). Usually, those sorts of numbers are a recipe for a beatdown. That the margin of victory wound up being four points, and that the Vikings had a lead with five minutes left to go in the game, is a testament to the effort the defense was able to put up before they finally just got worn down.

But this offense, quite simply, is just not a serious NFL offense right now. And, unfortunately, the path to any sort of a simple fix for this season just doesn't appear to be there.

There were those of us who spent this offseason screaming into the void that Kyler Murray was not a fit for what the Vikings have wanted to do offensively in the Kevin O'Connell era. Think, for a second, about the two quarterbacks who have really been successful in this offense since O'Connell became the head coach: Kirk Cousins and Sam Darnold. What did those guys do well?

Lined up under center, excelled in the play-action game, turned their back to the defense, didn't run around a lot, manipulated the pocket and fired passes down the field.

Or, to put it another way. . .roughly the exact opposite of everything Kyler Murray has done throughout his NFL career prior to now.

Per a September article from Garrett Burroughs over at Vikings Wire, during his time in Arizona, Murray was lined up in the shotgun on approximately 85% of the Cardinals' snaps, per numbers taken from Next Gen Stats. Since O'Connell became the Vikings' head coach in 2022, only two teams in the NFL had a lower percentage of snaps out of the shotgun than the Vikings' 53%.

The style of offense that O'Connell has wanted to run since he became the Vikings' head coach is not compatible with Murray's skill set, and whatever adjustments needed to be made apparently have not been. But, here we are, continuing to attempt to jam the square peg into the round hole with entirely predictable results.

And, respectfully, miss me with any sort of "Well, he had to split reps in training camp" excuse. Kyler Murray is approaching 100 career NFL starts. If he looks like this because he had to cede a few training camp reps. . .well, then there are a few other questions that need to be answered.

So, what's the fix? Honestly, I'm not sure if there is one.

There probably isn't a feasible trade scenario. Any quarterback that you're going to trade for at this point is probably going to require you to pay through the nose and will require an adjustment period of some sort. There is one notable exception, and man, if you think people have thoughts about the quarterback situation now, just wait until the potential premiere of Kirko 2: Kirk Harder.

Yes, Kirk Cousins could step into this offense immediately and be an upgrade. . .and, yes, I can't believe that's a sentence I'm typing in this, the year of our Lord 2026. But that comes with a hitch as well, that being that the Las Vegas Raiders have had the audacity to go out and actually be a competitive football team this season, largely due to Cousins' play.

Did you know that Kirk Cousins is currently second in the NFL in touchdown passes? He's thrown more than Josh Allen, more than Patrick Mahomes, more than Matthew Stafford, and more than anyone else not named Joe Burrow. And outside of Brock Bowers, I can't name three guys he's throwing the ball to without going to ESPN or Pro Football Reference or something. So while a Cousins trade would help the Vikings. . .do the Raiders even want to move him?

(Would it be wrong to point out that the Vikings could have signed Cousins this offseason? That would be wrong of me, wouldn't it? Okay, then, I won't do it.)

For better or worse, the Vikings may be locked into their current quarterback depth chart for the rest of this season. Maybe I'll be wrong on that, but I don't see anything else that does anything for them this season at the quarterback spot.

The Vikings have had other trade rumors around them as well, notably for Colts' running back Jonathan Taylor. Our friends at Stampede Blue have said that the asking price for Taylor is a first-round pick and a defensive tackle, which is a price that the Vikings should absolutely not be entertaining, in my opinion. Jonathan Taylor doesn't fix this offense if there's no passing game, and in its current state, the Vikings need to be careful about expending too much draft capital. Why?

Well, because this team has zero quarterbacks on the roster under contract beyond this season. Murray is here on a one-year deal and, as we know, hasn't been making what you'd call a super compelling case for being the long-term guy anyway. Carson Wentz is on a one-year deal and also isn't the long-term answer. And if you've looked at the 2027 free agent pool at the quarterback position, it's a bit of a wasteland. Even in the aftermath of the J.J. McCarthy situation. . .and don't get me started on that again. . .this team is probably going to have to take another swing at a quarterback in the draft sooner rather than later, and given that they already have six wins, if they want to make any sort of move for a top quarterback in 2027, they're going to need picks to do that.

I can understand Kevin O'Connell coming to the podium after games each week and telling us that the offense is close and that the breakthrough is coming any time now. I get it, honestly. But, you know. . .we're halfway through the 2026 season. At this point, you sort of are what you are. And, at this point, the Minnesota Vikings are a bottom-five NFL offense by pretty much any objective measure, and I'm not sure that there's a fix that's going to change that for the second half of this season.

But, as always, I'm more than open to Nolan Teasley and company proving me wrong.

#2685. Eagles vs. Commanders: Good, bad, and ugly from Philadelphia's loss

The Philadelphia Eagles finally gave their fans something to cheer about early Sunday night. Unfortunately, it didn't last long. A 10-0 first-quarter lead against the Washington Commanders turned into a 27-10 defeat, extending Philadelphia's losing streak to six games and adding another prime-time performance that offered more questions than answers.

This one was particularly frustrating because the Eagles showed flashes of the football they can play. They forced a turnover, found creative ways to score, and had chances to keep the game competitive. Sadly, those moments became increasingly difficult to find as the night progressed.

Philadelphia's opening 15 minutes were its most productive first quarter of the season. The Eagles had managed just 10 first-quarter points through their previous six games, including three against the Los Angeles Rams and seven against the Dallas Cowboys. They matched that total in one quarter against Washington, then disappeared offensively for the rest of the night.

Andrew Mukuba gave the Eagles an early spark when he punched the football loose from Commanders tight end Chig Okonkwo. Zack Baun recovered the fumble at Washington's 26-yard line. Philadelphia needed only three plays to turn the takeaway into a touchdown. Saquon Barkley finished the drive with a three-yard score on a direct snap out of the Wildcat formation.

Elijah Mitchell also showed a little burst in a limited opportunity. He finished with 34 yards on 11 carries, hardly a performance that will change the conversation about Philadelphia's running game, but there were moments when he looked capable of creating something with the ball. Eli Stowers gave the Eagles another small positive by recording his first three NFL receptions, finishing with 53 yards.

Marcus Epps deserves recognition, too. He isn't a perfect safety. He has his limits, but his effort rarely disappears. He recorded a well-timed pass breakup that helped Philadelphia avoid an even bigger problem after Washington threatened to turn a downfield completion into another damaging sequence. The defense also benefited from a roughing-the-passer penalty that erased a would-be interception after Dallas Goedert couldn't secure a catch. The crowd made its displeasure known, but it was the right call.

Then Tanner McKee scrambled for 15 yards to convert a third down. Let that sink in for a second. The quarterback isn't exactly known for making plays with his legs, but he found a way to move the chains when Philadelphia needed it.

The most encouraging message came afterward from Saquon Barkley. Asked about an ESPN report that the Eagles would not trade him and whether he wanted to remain in Philadelphia, he made his position clear.

"I would love to be here... I don't like the way the season's going. I'm not one of those guys that's like, 'Oh, the season's not going the way we (want). Let's just jump ship.' That's not the type of person you want to have, not the type of person I am. I've got to be part of, right now, we've got a problem we've got to fix. Hopefully, I'll be one of the reasons why we fix it."

Barkley is dealing with injuries. This season has been nothing like what he or Philadelphia expected, but his willingness to take responsibility and stay committed is exactly the kind of mentality this team needs right now.

A 10-point advantage disappeared before halftime. Washington scored 13 unanswered points in the second quarter, and the Eagles never recovered. McKee looked far less comfortable than he did against Dallas in Week 7, and one of Philadelphia's most promising drives ended with a costly strip sack.

McKee finished with 212 passing yards, no touchdowns, and an interception. Washington brought him down five times, and his struggle to handle pressure became increasingly apparent as the game wore on. The Eagles also struggled to create separation without their usual receiving options, making it harder to find answers when the offense needed a play.

Washington's 11-play, 89-yard touchdown drive showed how easily opposing offenses can move the ball against Philadelphia. Jayden Daniels completed five of six passes for 49 yards and added a 14-yard scramble up the middle. The Eagles generated little meaningful pressure, letting Washington dictate the possession and finish with a touchdown.

The Commanders entered the matchup as the league's worst team on third down. They weren't much better on Sunday night, but they were good enough. Philadelphia still allowed them to convert five of 13 attempts. The pass rush failed to consistently disrupt Daniels, and the return coverage kept giving opponents favorable field position. Washington opened the game with a 44-yard kickoff return and added a 27-yard punt return before halftime.

The offensive decision-making was just as frustrating. Philadelphia had a clearly placed Barkley on a pitch count, yet still put him in a situation where he was asked to take a half-ending carry on a possession that wasn't designed to be aggressive. There was little reason to expose an injured player to unnecessary contact in a moment that offered minimal upside.

The Eagles don't have much time to dwell on another loss. The New York Giants visit Lincoln Financial Field on Sunday, Nov. 8, and Philadelphia needs to make several important decisions before the week gets away from it. The first is at quarterback: Does McKee get another opportunity, or has the time arrived to seriously consider Joe Milton?

The coaching staff also needs a clearer plan to protect the quarterback and build an offense that can function under pressure. Thursday's practice will offer another important checkpoint on personnel availability, but the larger question is whether Philadelphia can put a more dependable group on the field and give it a plan that plays to its strengths.

The Giants game is the Eagles' final opportunity before their Week 10 bye to show that this season can still be redirected. Another loss would send them into the break with even more difficult questions and very little evidence that the current approach is working.

#2681. Report: Jaguars' DaVon Hamilton to miss rest of season with torn quad

Jacksonville Jaguars nose tackle DaVon Hamilton is expected to miss the remainder of the season after suffering a torn quad in the team's blowout win over the Indianapolis Colts on Sunday, per NFL Media's Ian Rapoport.

Rapoport said the defensive tackle will undergo more tests, but his season is over.

Hamilton exited the contest in the second quarter of Sunday's game while fighting through multiple blocks. The Jaguars recovered the fumble and defeated the Colts 42-7. He was quickly ruled out with what was then determined to be a knee injury.

Jaguars trade thoughts: They should swing for Jordan Davis, Budda Baker

Still, losing Hamilton will be a tough pill for Jacksonville's defense to swallow.

The Jaguars are ranked first in run defense, leading the league in multiple categories, including rushing yards allowed per game (77.4) and yards per carry allowed (3.39). The Jaguars have allowed just four rushing touchdowns this season through seven games.

The Jaguars drafted Hamilton in the third round of the 2020 NFL Draft and he has spent his entire career in Jacksonville. Hamilton has played in 93 games (68 starts), accounting for 260 tackles (131 solos), 18 tackles for loss, 22 quarterback hits, and six sacks. He also has two forced fumbles and four batted passes.

Hamilton is in the final year of a three-year, $34.5 million contract extension signed in April 2023.

Against the Colts Sunday, star running back Jonathan Taylor managed just 23 yards on eight carries after the team took a 28-0 lead at halftime.

#2676. How can Timberwolves survive Anthony Edwards' absence? LaMelo Ball must level up, but there's another key

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Minnesota Timberwolves superstar Anthony Edwards is expected to miss up to two months as he undergoes arthroscopic surgery on his ailing right knee, according to ESPN's Shams Charania.

This is stunning news, as it comes less than 24 hours after Edwards played like a superhero, scoring 47 points in an overtime loss to the Cleveland Cavaliers on Monday. Rather than have Edwards continue to play on the injured knee, the team decided to address the issue early in the season, with December as the target for Edwards' return, per The Athletic. The surgery is scheduled for Thursday, per ESPN.

This is the same knee that gave Edwards trouble last season and he was listed as questionable for Wednesday's game against the Golden State Warriors with "right knee injury maintenance" earlier Tuesday. He has since been downgraded to out.

Edwards, who was seen grabbing at his right knee during Sunday's win over the Toronto Raptors, missed the final game of Minnesota's first-round playoff win over the Denver Nuggets last year with a hyperextension to this same knee, but was able to return against the San Antonio Spurs for Game 1 of the conference semifinals off the bench.

This was from The Athletic's game story on Monday night:

"Edwards dealt with a hyperextended left knee in the playoffs last season and was also bothered by inflammation in his right knee. He played through it in inspiring fashion, getting around-the-clock treatment and having his right knee drained multiple times to stay available, and said in the preseason that he took most of two months off to allow both knees to heal."

It sure looked like that time he took off this summer had worked. The Wolves are 3-1 and were looking like one of the league's best teams behind the electric duo of Edwards and LaMelo Ball, who was acquired from the Charlotte Hornets in a June blockbuster.

Through the first week and change, Edwards is averaging 33.3 points per game and leading the league with 18 3-pointers at a 40% clip. He already has games of 45 and 47 points, and did so on a right knee that needs surgery.

The Wolves have to hold the fort down as best they can without Edwards, and their best chance at doing so in a deep Western Conference is for Ball to lead the offensive charge. Edwards is a two-way star. This will affect the Wolves' second-ranked defense, but there is more infrastructure in place on that side. Ball is Minnesota's best bet to continue creating quality offense and you'd have to imagine his scoring will tick up.

Take the tiny sample for what it's worth, but so far this season the Wolves are operating at what would be a bottom-10 offensive rate over 74 non-garbage-time possessions with Ball on the court without Edwards, per Cleaning the Glass. That will obviously need to improve.

Ball averaged over 20 points per game last year with the Hornets but is down to 14.8 this year. That's because Edwards has been so dominant, and Ball has been effective beyond his box scores by creating pace and energy. But now the Wolves need him to be more aggressive as a scorer (hopefully with some modicum of efficiency) and to prove he's ready to fully lead a team with real expectations.

That said, he doesn't have to do it alone. This is where it really hurts that Donte DiVincenzo is rehabbing a torn Achilles, but the Wolves still have a handful of guys who can add to the collective effort of at least somewhat replacing Edwards' production in the aggregate.

Terrence Shannon Jr. has been sensational to start the year. Jonathan Kuminga, who can create his own offense, has a real opportunity to put himself in his best light as he remains in search of the lucrative long-term contract that has eluded him. Ayo Dosunmu is a double-digit scorer and 3-point marksman who can level up.

But none of these guys can do what the Wolves' new No. 2 can.

McDaniels is currently on a five-year, $136 million contract and the Wolves just signed him to a one-year, $40 million extension to set as his base number for another potential extension in 2028. In other words, McDaniels makes All-Star money and could be on his way to more than that, and he's worth it. Now he's going to have to really be worth it.

McDaniels has All-Star upside, and with what should be a meaningful usage bump in Edwards' absence, this is his time to take the leap. He's averaging 15 points per game on 59% shooting so far. He's making 42% of his 3s. We know he's a demon defender, but he's been on a steady rise as a major offensive weapon who can create for himself (he has one of the best deceleration steps in the league).

As we saw during his time with Charlotte, Ball lifts the shooting of those around him as much as any player in the league. We've already seen that in Minnesota, too, and now that McDaniels is going to be even more of a target for Ball, he could easily jump north of 20 points per game and threaten for an All-Star spot.

Remember, this is a guy who went for 32 points and 10 boards to close out the Nuggets in Game 6 of their first-round series last year without Edwards, who was sidelined because of the same knee on which he's now set for surgery. McDaniels is a championship No. 3 option in the OG Anunoby mold, but he can be a legit No. 2 option for a "hold down the fort" stretch. It's time for him to prove it.

In Ball's case, ramping up to All-Star production is the expectation. He's been at that level before. But McDaniels joining him on that level is the key to Minnesota surviving Ant's absence.

Between now and Christmas, the Wolves have only six games against upper-echelon teams: the Spurs, Rockets, Knicks, Thunder, and the Lakers (twice).

They lose all margin for error against the Portlands and Memphis' of the league, but all things considered, this is a relatively soft stretch of schedule with 16 of their next 26 at home. Here's how it looks through November, a month that includes an eight-game homestand.

#2675. Jaguars' trade deadline plans are clear after DaVon Hamilton's season-ending injury

Jaguars' trade deadline plans are clear after DaVon Hamilton's season-ending injury originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

The Jacksonville Jaguars beat the Indianapolis Colts in Week 8, further cementing their status atop the AFC South. With the Colts collapsing, the Tennessee Titans at 1-7, and the Houston Texans underwhelming, the Jaguars are in great shape for the division.

But when it comes to making a deep playoff run, James Gladstone is going to need to find some more help. While Brian Thomas Jr. trade rumors continue to run rampant, the real intrigue with the Jaguars' deadline plans is what they're going to buy.

Unfortunately, according to NFL Network's Ian Rapoport, defensive tackle DaVon Hamilton suffered a season-ending injury, which has made it clear what the Jaguars are going to do this year by the NFL trade deadline.

"Sources: Jaguars standout DT DaVon Hamilton suffered a torn quad in Sunday's win over the Colts, and he's expected to be out for the season," Rapoport reported. "Hamilton will undergo more tests today, but a massive hole for Jacksonville."

As Rapoport noted, the loss of Hamilton leaves a massive hole along the team's interior defensive line. But it's even worse than that for the Jaguars.

They already needed defensive tackle help ahead of the 2026 NFL trade deadline. Jacksonville had been linked to multiple DT's in the trade market already before this injury occurred.

But now, with Hamilton done for the year, it couldn't be more obvious what the Jaguars are going to be looking to add this season by the NFL trade deadline: DT help.

MORE: Ravens' 6 best QB options to replace injured Lamar Jackson, from Jacoby Brissett to Shedeur Sanders

They already were looking for help, and now down a key player for the year, their need is that much more apparent. One obvious team to look at is the Philadelphia Eagles.

Moro Ojomo is a high-quality rental that, while he'd cost a bit to add, would be worth it. There are also rumors about Jalen Carter being available for trade, and while such a deal might cost two first-round picks, it's at least something Gladstone should check in on.

Ojomo is a lot more realistic for the Jaguars. There aren't a lot of good defensive tackles available for trade this year, and with multiple teams looking for help, it might become expensive to win a bidding war.

Jacksonville doesn't have a choice, unfortunately, as this Hamilton injury has really left them with a huge hole up front that needs to be resolved by this year's deadline.

It's obvious the Jaguars need DT help, and it might be a matter of when, not if, Gladstone swings a trade before the November 10 trade deadline.

#2674. Nick Martinez, bullpen save the Rays from World Series elimination, but Game 4 win merely a stay of execution

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. -- First things first: the Rays did what they had to do to win Game 4. Trailing 3-0 in the World Series means you do absolutely everything possible to survive and get to Game 5. You can't hold anything -- or anyone -- back because saving a pitcher for a game that never comes is a fool's errand.

I speak of Nick Martinez, the Rays' All-Star starter who was set to get the start in Game 5 of the World Series, if necessary. The Rays have had bullpen issues in the ALCS and World Series and desperately needed to keep this game under control from the feisty Brewers offense. Manager Kevin Cash was relying on a huge effort from Martinez and the rest of their bullpen.

He got it for most of the night, as Rays relievers worked eight of the 12 innings and allowed just one run on four hits. This was a night of redemption for that group. They had blown Game 1 of the ALCS, had trouble in Game 6 of that series, blew Game 2 of the World Series and were humiliated in Game 3. The mighty and relentless Brewers had been held at bay by the embattled group that seemed cooked just one night before.

And then the Rays walked it off in the 12th inning to win 4-3 and cut the Brewers' World Series deficit to 3-1.

Martinez has been a versatile guy throughout his career. In the regular season, he's made 160 starts and 151 appearances in relief. He's had most roles; he even had eight saves in a season once. He pitched in Japan for four seasons. He's done it all.

After throwing 73 pitches in five innings as the starter in Game 1 for the Rays, he was needed for six outs in this one. He was up to the task and held the Brewers in check.

"Gritty. Gritty. We're dangerous," Martinez said after the game. "We have our backs against the wall…we know what we have to do. We can win four in a row. This team is capable of doing that."

Credit also goes to Rays closer Bryan Baker. He's had velocity issues and hadn't thrown more than an inning at a timesince Aug. 17. He worked two scoreless in this one. Kevin Kelly, Tyler Wells and Cam Booser also deserve to be shouted out for their scoreless work. Ian Seymour coughed up the go-ahead home run in the 12th, but that was all the damage he allowed, giving his team the shot to come back and win in the bottom of the inning.

"I can't say enough about Nick Martinez and the contributions he's made all season long. Then coming in on short rest and giving us two really solid innings," Cash said after the game. "Also Bryan Baker, those of you that follow us know that we generally keep Bake to one inning. We knew we have to win this game. His two innings were very helpful.

"We're going to get together after this session and sit down and talk about pitching. Going to check who's available. I'm going to guess most guys are going to say they're capable of an inning or more given it's Game 5 of the World Series, but nothing has been decided yet."

There are good vibes now in the Rays clubhouse for the first time this series. They avoided the sweep.

Was this just a reprieve or, even grimmer, a stay of execution? The Brewers have Jacob Misiorowski waiting in the wings to start Game 5. The Rays have a giant question mark.

Would they really turn around and start Martinez on zero days of rest after he threw 33 pitches in Game 4? Drew Rasmussen got knocked around pretty good in Game 2 and would be on short rest. His numbers on short rest in his career are awful (five runs in seven innings in four starts). Freddy Peralta just threw Game 3 and Griffin Jax started Game 4.

It's really shaping up like a bullpen game and, for all the good that mentioned above, keep in mind just how shaky the Rays' bullpen has been outside of Tuesday night. The Rays are probably pretty well screwed for Game 5.

Now, to be clear, in no way am I blaming Cash for burning Martinez. He absolutely had to do it. Too many of the bullpen alternatives inspired a low level of confidence after what we've seen recently. It felt inevitable that the Brewers were going to crush one of them. Again, you can't figure out Game 5 if you lose Game 4 and get swept. So Cash used Martinez and Baker for four innings combined and it worked well masterfully.

Will be both available for Game 5? Maybe! The Rays are still facing elimination and everything needs to be on the table. It just looks like they'll be at a sizable disadvantage.

The vibes are high in the home clubhouse in Tropicana Field, but for how long? Yeah, I'll call it a stay of execution. Kudos to the Rays for extending the series, but the Brewers are going to close things down in Game 5.

#2670. Jacob Misiorowski's moment? MLB's most electric starter can pitch the Brewers to their first title

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — In the bowels of Tropicana Field early Wednesday morning, Jacob Misiorowski wouldn't even break stride.

Much like his 105-mph fastball that devastates hitters and leaves observers in awe, Misiorowski moved through the crowded corridor, littered with fans, in a blur.

"Miz!" one fan yelled, reaching for a fist bump.

But Misiorowski never extended his hand. His acknowledgment came in the form of a head nod, his attention seemingly fixed on what awaited him later that evening.

For Misiorowski will take the mound Wednesday night with a chance to clinch Milwaukee's first World Series championship.

The Brewers squandered their first opportunity at history in Game 4, when Tampa Bay's Ben Williamson delivered a walk-off single in the bottom of the 12th inning. Williamson's chopper capped a two-run Rays' rally that erased Milwaukee's one-run lead and forced Wednesday's Game 5.

"When you're achieving something like this, it's going to have its adversity," manager Pat Murphy said. "We had some things go our way yesterday. They had some things go their way today. That's the way it is. You just live with it, and if you're a competitor, you wake up tomorrow morning and come ready to play."

Isn't this what the Fall Classic is about?

Letting superstars be superstars? Giving them the stage to carry their teams to baseball's ultimate glory?

Milwaukee's Cooper Pratt nearly authored his own piece of history Tuesday night. His solo home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th had all the makings of a storybook ending. A rookie. Just 22 years old. Delivering on his promise six months after signing a contract extension.

Pratt's night, which included three other hits, showed that the bonds holding this Brewers club together aren't rooted solely in veteran leaders like Christian Yelich and William Contreras. Or in Murphy and Milwaukee's relentless approach to the game. But also in a rookie who has enjoyed success while enduring his share of defensive growing pains.

This Brewers club is the sum of its parts.

Misiorowski is the Brewers' brightest star. One of the most unique starters the game has ever seen, it's all but certain he will win the NL Cy Young Award in a few weeks.

But throughout Milwaukee's dominant eight-game winning streak this October, finally snapped by Tampa Bay, Misiorowski's impact has amounted to little more than a fist bump when compared with the firm handshake of his teammates.

His impact hasn't truly been felt. His dominance hasn't fully manifested.

His first postseason start, against the Padres in the NLDS, lasted just four innings. His second, against the Dodgers, went only 4⅓. He was better in Game 1 of the World Series, lasting five innings. But now it's time for a Cy Young-caliber performance.

And with a championship hanging in the balance, the Brewers are handing him the baseball.

Jacob Misiorowski has been good but not his level of great in these 2026 MLB playoffs

The Rays did everything in their power to survive Game 4. That's what happens when you're down 3-0 in the World Series. Desperation mounts with each passing inning, particularly when the game hangs in the balance.

Manager Kevin Cash turned to Nick Martinez, his scheduled starter for Wednesday evening. He burned through closer Bryan Baker for two innings and Ian Seymour for another. Cameron Booser recorded just one out in his second consecutive appearance.

The Brewers, meanwhile, could have gone for the kill.

Aaron Ashby worked 2⅓ scoreless innings beginning in the ninth, continuing his marvelous postseason. But when Murphy removed him with one out in the 11th, it became clear that Milwaukee's manager wasn't willing to sacrifice tomorrow for today.

"I had an idea of why he was coming out to get me," he said. "He saw my last fastball, and I knew that was going to be on their mind."

"He was disappointed he was coming out," he said. "But I said we've got to be mindful of your health, and we've got to be mindful of winning the whole thing. If you're going to win the whole thing, you have to understand that we can't drain you today or risk injury today. He's thrown a lot."

Murphy never considered bringing in Misiorowski. Not in that situation. The risk was too great.

"You can't blow that type of situation on a one-run lead on the road," Murphy continued. "If we were in the 13th inning and we had a three-run lead, that might have been a little bit different. Probably still wouldn't have."

From the start. Where Misiorowski belongs.

With the world watching. With Milwaukee's first World Series championship within reach. And with the baseball in the hands of the Brewers' 24-year-old superstar.

For much of this postseason, Misiorowski has remained in the background.

His dominance hasn't fully manifested. Now it's time for his moment.

"That loss stinks," Ashby said. "But it's part of our story. I think the boys are fired up to get back in there Wednesday."

And surely, that fan would rather celebrate a World Series championship delivered by Misiorowski than receive a fist bump from him.

#2669. NBA Power Rankings: Rockets take over No. 1 spot with sublime start, Heat take huge tumble

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

When the Houston Rockets' preseason win total line came out a 48.5, I had to wipe my glasses and check again. Vegas doesn't make mistakes. And if that's the line, I realize that's where the sportsbooks are getting the right balance of wagers. So, apparently, the betting public didn't get it, because this is a team that won 52 games last season despite not having a point guard and being sans Steven Adams for the second half of their schedule.

Everyone remembers the Houston team that went out with a postseason whimper and, outside of begging Kevin Durant to make contested jumpers, looked borderline inept in the half-court. But the Rockets were still the No. 8 offense and No. 6 defense a season ago. They went 1-7 in overtime games. The 52 wins were about the worst outcome possible, and with Fred VanVleet and Adams back ... their line was 48.5?

It seemed like too easy of a bet, and through the first week of the season, it still does. The Rockets are 4-0 and look like an entirely different offense. Durant has talked about the difference VanVleet has made in allowing the Rockets to slot back into their collectively comfortable positioning. No more point guard by committee, which allows Durant to operate more off ball. Last year he had to initiate pick-and-roll offense on almost 18% of his possessions, per Synergy, but this year that's down to 7.3% while his spot-up and transition rates are up.

That's easier offense for him, and he's currently averaging 23.5 points on 54/47 shooting splits. But Durant is going to make shots in any offense. It's the other guys that are benefiting from the improved spacing and flow. Amen Thompson and Jabari Smith Jr. are catching on the move and flying downhill. Houston is up three assists a game from last year and is creating almost 10 more points per game off those assists. Last year, they were in the bottom 10 in total passes per game. This year they're in the top 10.

Alperen Sengun is initiating offense as a high hub, and it puts defenses in an almost impossible spot. He's huge and is going to bully pretty much any defender one-on-one to the rim, but if you come to help Durant is spotting up or some long athlete is running to the rim. Sengun is picking defenses apart at 24.5 points, nine boards and seven assists per game on 58% shooting. Give him space at the top, and he'll exploit that, too. He's made six of nine 3-pointers so far.

Reed Sheppard brings even more juice. When he's in the game, it's a different look with him running off two-man actions and hunting shots without the burden of trying to operate as an offensive organizer. It speaks to all of the different ways the Rockets are stressing defenses right now. There's real diversity here, and with it, a real shot at contending for a suddenly wide-open Western crown.

Think about it: The Thunder just lost Jalen Williams for the season, and Cason Wallace is also out for an extended period with a torn labrum. The Timberwolves are likely going to be without Anthony Edwards through Christmas, while the Spurs are still trying to figure out their lineups with three guards and Victor Wembanyama not looking like the world-wrecking force everyone predicted, at least not yet. This might be a one-year opportunity for a team like Houston to push all its chips in and go for broke.

And they have the chips to do it. They have all kinds of draft capital and plenty of young talent to put together a package for just about any available player in the league. If VanVleet's mere presence has lifted this team as it has, imagine De'Aaron Fox or Kyrie Irving running point. I doubt the Spurs would want to strengthen a direct competitor with a in-season Fox move, but an Irving deal is perfect for both sides.

He's not on the Mavericks' timeline, and this is an opportunity to add more draft picks to build around Cooper Flagg and kick the tires on a Reed Sheppard future inside-out pairing. They could get Smith out of the deal, too, I would imagine. I think Houston is a shadow contender as constructed, but you add a guy like Kyrie and this team has a real shot. There would never be a better time than now.

And with that, let's get to this week's power rankings, where the Rockets sit at No. 1 after one week of the 2026-27 NBA season.

#2668. ‘I think we’ve had enough’: Legendary coach sends a message to Donald Trump during long rally

President Donald Trump has never been known for keeping his rallies short. So when one of the most legendary coaches in sports history took the microphone in Iowa on Sunday, he decided to do a little clock management.

Former Iowa wrestling coach Dan Gable joined Trump on stage at the rally and kept his remarks extremely brief. And his opening line made it sound like he thought the crowd had heard enough at the rally.

Trump was in Iowa on Sunday to campaign for Senate candidate Ashley Hinson, with the midterm elections just two days away. The rally was another long one, with Trump going on yet another rant about the NFL's kickoff rule and calling football "boring as hell."

Gable is about as big a name as there is in Iowa. He won 15 NCAA team titles as Iowa's head coach and won Olympic gold in 1972 without surrendering a single point. His Iowa teams won nine straight national championships from 1978 to 1986, a run that still makes him a household name in the state.

He also has a history with Trump. Trump awarded Gable the Presidential Medal of Freedom in December 2020.

When Gable got his turn to speak, he seemingly made it pretty clear that he felt the rally was going a little too long.

"I think we've had enough. I'm a pretty good coach, and I read everything really well," Gable said, in a clip shared by Rapid Response 47.

Gable then kept his own words brief as he offered a quick endorsement before handing things back over.

"This guy's doing the job that needs to be done. That's my coaching expertise, and I'm a pretty damn good coach. Thank you," he said.

Gable was clearly there to support Trump. But his brief remarks quickly went viral, with plenty of people online taking his opening line as a not-so-subtle hint that it was time to wrap things up.

Rapid Response 47 left the "I think we've had enough" line out of its caption, focusing instead on Gable's praise.

"I don't feel welcome when I go there, you know? Even in spring training, I don't feel like -- I'm just like, I don't know, I don't feel welcome. I don't feel like they want me there, so I don't go."

Posada, a four-time World Series champion with New York, did not elaborate on his comments or cite a specific incident that made him feel unwelcome in the organization.

Posada, now 56, first signed with the Yankees after they made him a 24th-round pick in 1990. He spent his entire professional career in pinstripes. Posada's MLB career with the Yankees lasted from 1995 through 2011. Over that span, he compiled 1,664 hits, 275 home runs, 936 walks, 1,065 RBI and a WAR of 42.7. Along the way, Posada earned five All-Star selections as the Yankees' primary catcher and twice finished in the top 10 of the American League MVP vote.

In 2015, the Yankees retired Posada's No. 20.

Since retiring as a player, Posada has held a number of baseball jobs, including a front office role with the Miami Marlins when his former Yankees teammate Derek Jeter was atop the club's front office.

As for his former team, the Yankees were recently eliminated from the postseason by the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series. The Yankees have not won the World Series since 2009, when Posada was still their starting catcher and still one of the team's leading contributors.

#2665. Celtics star Jayson Tatum says he's 'starting to feel like my old self' again after hitting game-winner

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Eighteen months out from a torn Achilles that cost him the majority of last season, Jayson Tatum said he's "really starting to feel like my old self" after burying a buzzer beater to lift the Boston Celtics to a thrilling 125-124 overtime win over the Brooklyn Nets on Tuesday.

Tatum finished with 40 points, eight assists and five rebounds on 10-of-20 shooting from the field, made a career-high 18 free throws and did not commit a single turnover. He now has seven game-winning shots with three or fewer seconds remaining in the 2020s, which is the most by any player this decade.

With 2.3 seconds remaining in overtime, the Celtics had the ball thanks to a bizarre decision by Nets rookie Mikel Brown Jr. to take a contested layup instead of waiting to be fouled. Everyone knew the ball was going to Tatum in that situation, and he took the inbound pass from Derrick White, spun to his left, took two dribbles and rose up for a wide-open free-throw line jumper that caught nothing but net and sent TD Garden into hysterics.

"I'm 18 months out [from the torn Achilles]. For me, it's about progress and how I'm moving," Tatum said on the broadcast after the game. "It's little moments throughout the game where I do something, and it's not always with the ball, where I'm like, 'Ooh, it's coming back to me and I'm really starting to feel like my old self.' I feel really good about that."

HAVE YOURSELF A NIGHT, JAYSON TATUM!☘️ 40 PTS ☘️ 8 AST☘️ 5 REB☘️ 1 @TISSOT BUZZER-BEATER IN OTTonight marks his 7th career game-winning shot with under 3 seconds remaining... that's the most since the start of the 2019-20 NBA season! pic.twitter.com/I0du5uQhvS

"We got the ball to the MVP, and he took us home," Tatum's new teammate Paul George said.

This was Tatum's 30th career 40-point game, which is tied for the second-most in Celtics history behind Larry Bird (47), and his fourth 40-point game without a turnover. Every other player in Celtics history has four such games combined.

"It was a hell of a feeling, just kind of getting back to doing things that I used to do before I was injured and sharing that moment with my teammates on the court," Tatum said during his postgame press conference. "Seeing them rally and be excited for me."

The first week of the season has been a roller coaster for Tatum, who shot 6 of 23 from the field in the Celtics' season-opening loss to the Detroit Pistons, in which they blew a 22-point lead, and has had to deal with off-court drama regarding his relationship with former teammate Jaylen Brown.

But on the court, he's been terrific since that first game and has looked more than capable of carrying the new-look Celtics. He poured in 36 points and hit a barrage of clutch jumpers to secure a win over the reigning champion New York Knicks on Oct. 23, and is averaging 33 points, seven rebounds, seven assists and 1.3 steals on 49.2% shooting in the last three games -- all Celtics wins.

"I've been in his position, being out from an injury," George said. "You come back to the game, you see the game differently. I've been saying it. From what I see, it's a maturity. You see a mature JT out there. Makes the right plays. Not only is he scoring and scoring efficiently, but he's making the right plays, he's getting assists, he's getting guys involved. He knows the attention that he draws and he's making the right plays. The game looks like it's slowing down and he's in that zone of seeing plays ahead of time."

#2662. Dakar mash-up combines Swiss and Senegalese wrestling traditions

At the entrance to a dirt field between buildings in a Dakar suburb, a Senegalese guide scatters salt into the air, then onto the ground ahead of Swiss wrestlers who one by one break into a run.

As part of a cultural exchange, three Senegalese and three Swiss wrestlers faced off Sunday in Dakar, mixing their own ancestral wrestling traditions.

The event was organised on the sidelines of the Youth Olympic Games which opened in Senegal on Saturday, marking the first ever Olympics on African soil.

The encounter started with the Swiss wrestlers trading in their usual getups for Senegalese wrestling attire.

In Switzerland, traditional wrestling known as "Schwingen" is practised wearing thick sackcloth shorts over trousers, with a wrestler grabbing hold of an opponent's shorts in an attempt to throw the fighter off balance and pin the person to the ground.

In Dakar, the wrestlers encountered a different attire.

Senegalese wrestling, known as "laamb", is performed bare-chested and in a loincloth, with the participant often adorned in "gris-gris", charms and amulets believed to offer protection.

To ensure their loincloths were tied correctly, the Swiss wrestlers received help from a Senegalese wrestling star, Emile Francois Gomis, known as "Franc".

Next came a mystical bath ritual: a little bit of water poured over the body, part of a protective tradition that some Senegalese wrestlers undergo.

Then drums started to beat and the singing of traditional songs began.

The Senegalese wrestlers entered, draped in traditional "leppi" cloth wraps.

The initial rounds featured young wrestlers, with the crowd cheering them on.

Then Modou Lo, a Senegalese wrestling legend and local resident, appeared to shouts and applause.

Together with his proteges, he performed a dance to the beat of percussions, and the Swiss wrestlers joined in, drawing further applause.

Then came the laamb matches, with the Senegalese naturally prevailing.

Swiss wrestler Matthieu Burger said his opponent "does it all the time, for me it's the first time. And he was stronger".

But he described the match as "great fighting, conducted with mutual respect".

The main difference, in his opinion, was that Swiss wrestling entails maintaining a constant grip on one's opponent, whereas there is more distance between wrestlers in Senegal.

Burger said he was confident the experience would prove useful in his own traditional wrestling.

Next, the roles were reversed: Senegalese wrestlers put on traditional burlap shorts to try their hand at Swiss wrestling, with the Swiss avenging their earlier defeat.

For "Franc", who initiated the event, the mission was accomplished: "This is what we wanted, to come and show Senegalese culture, our pride. Wrestling, it's our sport," he said.

The Senegalese style, with its raw power and rituals, and Swiss style, with its rigour and centuries-old history, serve as a "cultural and sporting bridge", said Aboubacar Djamil Sane, mayor of Dakar's Parcelles Assainies municipality, where the event took place.

On the Swiss side, Patricia Danzi, a former Olympian who is representing the Swiss government at the Youth Olympic Games as the director general of the Swiss Agency for Development and Cooperation, said she was moved.

The Games, she said, "don't just take place in the stadiums, they also happen in our neighbourhoods".

#2661. NBA one-week overreactions: Luka Dončić as the MVP frontrunner? Who's in the most trouble?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The NBA season is underway and chaos already abounds. The Grizzlies are one of three undefeated teams atop the Western Conference; the Heat are winless and in disarray; and there has been a rash of major injuries to superstars across the league, raising countless questions about how teams go forward from here.

Given all that, it's time for our overreactions from the season's first week.

This isn't even an overreaction. The season has barely begun, and there's already been an endless string of serious injuries to big-name players. Anthony Edwards and Kawhi Leonard were the latest of the bunch. On Tuesday, news emerged that Edwards will undergo arthroscopic surgery on his right knee and miss up to two months. That's a huge blow for the Wolves, who were off to a 3-1 start. Now, Minnesota will have to figure out a way to stay afloat without Edwards, who was the second leading scorer in the NBA behind only Luka Dončić. Meanwhile, the Raptors will be without Leonard for "a period of weeks" while he deals with swelling in his right knee.

It continues. The Jazz will be without Jaren Jackson Jr. for six to eight weeks after he tore his MCL. The Magic lost Paolo Banchero for four to six weeks with a right ankle sprain, as well as Jalen Suggs, who will be re-evaluated in two weeks after bruising his right knee. Pistons center Jalen Duren is out at least two weeks with a hamstring strain. Kristaps Porziņģis, Kon Knueppel and AJ Dybantsa have yet to play for their respective teams due to various injuries/health issues. And after sitting out all of last season, Ben Simmons blew out his Achilles before playing a single regular-season minute for the Kings.

And then there are the Thunder. Jalen Williams played just 33 games last season but returned healthy and ready to go this year -- only to suffer a dislocated ankle and a fractured fibula against the Clippers over the weekend. If you haven't seen it, don't search for it. It was the kind of gruesome scene that made many people recall the awful and unforgettable injuries previously suffered by Gordon Hayward and Paul George. The Thunder haven't officially declared Williams done for the season, but it would be surprising if he recovered from significant surgery in time to return. Oklahoma City also lost Cason Wallace with a torn labrum. Same situation there in terms of facing long odds on bouncing back from surgery in time to play this season or postseason.

The NBA is at its most enjoyable when the brightest stars are available to shine on the court. This is a dark start.

Deep breath, Thunder fans. No one wanted to see OKC lose Williams and Wallace. It was a brutal blow for the players and the team. Adding another injury to the ever-growing list, Alex Caruso -- who was expected to play increased minutes and take on more responsibility with two of the Thunder's best defenders on the mend -- made it just nine minutes into their game against the Suns before spraining his ankle. He's already listed as out for Wednesday's outing in Dallas and is expected to miss some time.

It's hard to imagine a worse scenario for the Thunder, who began the season with the best odds to win the NBA title. But even with those unwelcome developments, OKC is still among the betting favorites to make a deep run this postseason. The Thunder (+380 at FanDuel) are second behind only the Spurs (+280) to win the Western Conference and the NBA Finals. That has everything to do with what Sam Presti has constructed in Oklahoma City. The Thunder are the deepest team in the league -- and now that premise will be tested.

Ajay Mitchell -- who began the season on the shortlist for Sixth Man of the Year candidates -- will be called upon to provide a scoring boost in the absence of Williams. (Mitchell is already off to a good start there, scoring an efficient career-high 30 points in 25 minutes in a win over the Suns on Monday.) The same goes for Jared McCain, who has morphed from a luxury addition following a trade with the 76ers last season to a critical component this year. You can also imagine Mark Daigneault leaning more on his bigs with Chet Holmgren, Isaiah Hartenstein and rookie Aday Mara. Jaylin Williams and another rookie, Bennett Stirtz, will have to gobble up minutes off the bench. And as always, the whole thing revolves around Shai Gilgeous-Alexander. Losing two players as important and talented as Williams and Wallace is an unlucky and unwanted turn of events, but as long as the reigning two-time MVP is on the floor, OKC remains formidable. If any team can handle this kind of strife, it's the Thunder.

Hey, look at that: New York finally won a game. The Knicks beat the Pistons at home on Tuesday, which undoubtedly came as a relief to them and their fans. New York started the season with three duds, losing at home on ring/banner night to the Sixers, falling in Boston to the Celtics, and then faceplanting at home to a Magic team that was without Banchero. Not how they wanted to begin their title defense.

The 0-3 start was the worst beginning to a follow-up season by the reigning champs since the Mavericks dropped their initial three games 15 years ago. When you win the first championship in 53 years, you can be forgiven for enjoying yourself over the summer and being distracted by the spotlight. It also probably didn't help their focus that the team paused negotiations with Karl Anthony-Towns and Josh Hart, or that the organization initially duped employees with a championship ring email that was actually a cybersecurity test (before later realizing how bad the optics are on that kind of thing and promising to retroactively make it right).

The good news, to the extent that there is any when you only win one of your first four games, is that Towns has played well so far -- he's averaging 22.5 points and 14 rebounds on 60.3% shooting from the floor -- even while the rest of the team has been largely inconsistent. The upcoming schedule is also encouraging. Over their next seven games, the Knicks play the Bulls twice, as well as the Nets and Bucks. After that, they have a road trip featuring games in Toronto (without Kawhi) and Minnesota (sans Edwards).

The Knicks still have quite a bit of work to do to return to form, but finally securing that first win did "a lot" for their psyche, as a relieved Jalen Brunson acknowledged after beating the Pistons.

You know things aren't going well when your three-time former MVP picks a fight with the fans -- and then doubles down. The Nuggets are 1-2. After Denver completed a 23-point comeback to barely beat the Pelicans at home in overtime, for the team's only win of the season, Nikola Jokić called out the fans for having the audacity to call out the Nuggets.

"I think those fans that booed, they don't need to come anymore," Jokic said. "If you guys follow us, you know that we never quit and we came back from much worse for similar situations. So if they ask me, they are not welcome anymore."

Nikola Jokic has a message for the fans that were booing the Nuggets in the first half:"They are not welcome anymore." pic.twitter.com/cZR2cr5ku7

Given a chance later to walk that back, Joker followed it up by saying he was sticking to his original point: "I think they are not real fans." Maybe this is an offshoot of the European soccer ethos that encourages supporters to rally behind their team when they let in a goal or get in a tough spot. Or maybe Jokić is just in his feelings about the Nuggets playing like garbage on the whole to start the season. As a native Philadelphian, it's always amusing to me when players get sore about people letting them know that they're not performing well. The easy solution is to perform better and the boos will abate. Problem solved.

Unfortunately for the Nuggets and their sensitivities, they followed up that win over the Pelicans by getting smoked by 20 on their own floor by the Warriors. Not ideal.

Yes, Golden State topped the Nuggets in Denver for its only win of the season, but that's only one more victory than the winless Pelicans and Kings have mustered. Not exactly the kind of company the Warriors want to keep. Golden State lost its opener at the Lakers, fell at home to the Grizzlies, then took another L on the road in Phoenix. Through their first four games, the Warriors were 19th in net rating and looking lost. The question is how they find their way, or if that's even possible.

Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg has been one of the few bright spots in the Bay. He's second on the team in points per game behind only Steph Curry, and he leads the Warriors in rebounds per game and verbal altercations with rival MVP candidates. (That last bit is saying something considering Draymond Green is still employed by the Warriors.)

The question is whether reinforcements will arrive in time to turn the Warriors into a competitive team and give them a shot at the play-in (sorry, Warriors fans but the playoffs proper look awfully far away right now). Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody are both recovering from knee injuries and it's uncertain when they might be able to return and contribute. Meanwhile, Porziņģis is reportedly contemplating his future in basketball while dealing with health concerns. It doesn't seem like the Warriors should expect any of them back anytime soon -- or, in the case of Porziņģis, who just got a new two–year contract worth $40 million -- possibly at all.

Curry also signed a new deal this offseason: a two-year. $115 million extension. That was less than he could have demanded in order to give the Warriors increased flexibility and options to put a better team around him. He'll be 39 in March. Time is not on his side, and neither is this Warriors roster.

Woof. The Heat are 0-4. They got blown out at home on opening night courtesy of the Wolves, then followed that up with losses to the Pistons, Hornets and Mavericks. This is obviously not what the Heat or Giannis Antetokounmpo had in mind when he left Milwaukee for South Beach.

"I said what needed to be said to the media," Antetokounmpo said. "Like we all have to take a deep breath and eventually we're going to figure it out, we cannot press the panic button… It's only going to get worse if you start panicking, man. I've been in this position before. I lost five in a row, I lost seven in a row… I don't like this feeling, the moment we turn this around  -- I'm going to always remember this feeling and I'm going try to not get back to this feeling."

Giannis Antetokounmpo: You cannot press the panic button and panic.....I don't like this feeling pic.twitter.com/yATRFvJA1N

When your current awful start makes you recall other dreadful stretches where you dropped five or seven games in a row, you're in a bad spot. It's also not a good sign when one of your starters says exactly what Heat fans don't want to hear and had convinced themselves all offseason wouldn't be the case. After Miami acquired Antetokounmpo, critics wondered about the floor spacing and shooting around him -- or more accurately about the lack of those things given the roster construction. Just this week, Davion Mitchell underlined those very concerns, especially as they pertain to Antetokounmpo and his fit with longtime Heat fan favorite Bam Adebayo.

"I think I got to do a better job of not letting [Adebayo] get lost in the game," Mitchell said after Monday's loss to Dallas. "He got to be more aggressive. I think that he will. He's still trying to figure it out because I said this before -- I think him and Giannis play in the same spaces, and then when Giannis is on the floor, he's on the floor. He can't be in those spaces."

Mitchell isn't wrong. But it's not solely on Adebayo. Antetokounmpo is just as much to blame for the clunky offense.

I don't like this right here...Bam gets the post up but Giannis decides to walk in the paint which gives Bam 0 space to work with.We gotta be smarter man. pic.twitter.com/84SwpMvDBY

Adebayo admitted his shot is "not going in" at present, then complained about how "the outside noise wants to make me the scapegoat." At least he's taking this well.

What was that about Giannis saying it wasn't time to press the panic button?

Last week, Dončić put out an open letter to the fans, promising no excuses and no days off. Some of us were skeptical about that. Since then, Dončić has done his talking on the court. That includes the first 50-point game of the NBA season and a historic night that etched his name in the Lakers' already overpacked record book.

LUKA JUST ERUPTED FOR 52 POINTS 🚨🪄 52 PTS🪄 8 REB🪄 10 AST🪄 2 STL🪄 8 3PM🪄 LAKERS ROAD WINHe becomes the first player in @Lakers franchise history to record 50+ PTS, 10+ AST, 5+ REB, and 5+ 3PM in a single game! pic.twitter.com/mfUAJSEJYB

The oddsmakers have Victor Wembanyama as the frontrunner, followed by Gilgeous-Alexander, then Dončić. That makes sense. But Wemby started the season by publicly declaring he was overthinking things (before course correcting and feasting on the hapless Kings on Tuesday night), and SGA could very well be the latest MVP unseated by voter fatigue, even if he has another impressive season while trying to carry the injury-impacted Thunder. Imagine a scenario where Dončić keeps dropping monster numbers for a new-look Lakers team that defies expectations and finishes higher in the Western Conference standings than anyone outside of LA could have predicted. Add in the Lakers allure and if he can stack stats and wins early, he moves to the front of the line.

Stop me if you've heard this before. When Joel Embiid is unavailable, the Sixers don't have a good solution for the giant hole he leaves in the frontcourt. That evergreen truth was further complicated when Philly lost Ariel Hukporti to an Achilles injury before the season even began. Following that development, coach Nick Nurse rattled off a litany of names who might see some time at the five, including LeBron James. That sounded good in theory -- but not so good to James in practice. When Embiid sat the second night of a back-to-back, James started as a small-ball center in a loss to the Pistons, then explained why that wasn't a long-term fix.

"Well, s--- we got an MVP over there. I'm not here to have a sustainable role at the 5," James said. "You got Joel Embiid on the team. ... If I was to say I was signed here to have a sustainable role at the 5, I don't think none of us would actually want that. I can do it, but... we have [Embiid]."

They have Embiid, yes. On paper. Sometimes even on the floor. But as everyone is painfully aware, especially and including the Sixers, Embiid's availability is subject to review. He's missed 150 games over the previous three seasons. That necessitates a contingency plan. James might not want to be part of it, but extenuating circumstances sometimes force people into undesirable situations. As ever, it's something to monitor for the Sixers going forward.

If they have any chance of actually competing for a championship, they'll need to stay afloat -- or at least not drown -- during the non-Embiid minutes and games. That might mean James doing something he doesn't want to do. But hey, at least James is having a good time with his new teammates.

#2659. Biggest questions for World Series Game 5: How will the Rays get enough innings to avoid elimination (again)?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Tampa Bay Rays took their first step toward a baseball miracle with their 12th-inning comeback win over the Milwaukee Brewers in Tuesday's Game 4 of the World Series. That 4-3 victory means the Rays avoided the sweep and cut the Brewers' series lead to 3-1. That sets the stage for Wednesday's Game 5.

Tuesday's escape for the Rays was obviously an essential one, as it was an elimination game. The win also nudged the Rays' chances of winning the series from "all but impossible" to "merely a longshot." Across all of Major League Baseball postseason history, 42 teams have been down 3-0, and only one – the 2004 Boston Red Sox – has come back to win the series in question. That is, history suggests the Rays had a mere 2.4% chance of pulling off the miracle comeback when they were down 3-0. Now, though, they're down 3-1.

In all, 96 teams have been down 3-1 in a best-of-seven MLB postseason series, and 14 of them have clawed back to win the series. That particular data set says the Rays have a 14.6% chance of stunning the Brewers and winning this Fall Classic. Those aren't great odds, obviously, but they're much better than the odds the Rays were facing going into Game 4. Interestingly, teams down 3-1 have a .500 record in Game 5.

Speaking of which, that brings us to three questions for Game 5 – the answers to which will determine whether the Rays can cut the Brewers' advantage to 3-2 and send the series back to Milwaukee. Let's get to it.

Here's the big one. Rays manager Kevin Cash wisely managed Game 4 for what it was: a must-win contest. That means you worry about tomorrow when tomorrow comes and tactically do everything possible to survive the elimination game. Tomorrow, though, has now arrived, and Cash must figure out how to deploy his pitching staff for another elimination game after using seven arms on Tuesday. Game 2 starter Drew Rasmussen will be going on short rest in Game 5, but what then?

The most notable Game 4 decision was using Nick Martinez, who had been slated to start Game 5, in relief. Martinez worked two scoreless innings out of the bullpen and threw 33 pitches. It'll be another all-hands-on-deck affair on Wednesday, but just who those hands will be after Rasmussen is another matter. Griffin Jax started Game 4 for Tampa Bay and amassed 74 pitches, which presumably rules him out for Game 5.

As for the traditional relievers, Cole Sulser, Steven Matz, and Garrett Cleavinger did not pitch on Tuesday and thus can probably expect to be used in Game 5. Bryan Baker and Kevin Kelly did pitch in Game 4 but they didn't pitch in Monday's Game 3 blowout loss, which means they're presumably available. Ian Seymour also didn't pitch in Game 3, but his 32-pitch workload in Game 4 may rule him out. Tyler Wells and Cameron Booser have each pitched two days in a row, but desperate straits in October may mean they'll be called upon again. As for Rasmussen, he's made short-rest starts before, but he was basically an opener in those outings, the last of which was in 2022. This, then, is something close to virgin territory for him. No doubt, Cash won't lean on Rasmussen for a long start even if he's cruising, but they could use some bulk from him given the shallow and probably tired bullpen. This will be Rasmussen's fifth start of the 2026 postseason. Across his previous four starts, he put up a 2.19 ERA and 2.57 FIP with 27 strikeouts and five walks in 24 ⅔ innings.

In light of the maxed-out stakes involved, anyone who's even a remotely feasible option will probably tell Cash he's willing to pitch. As such, Cash's decisions on whom to trust and whom to assign the plurality of innings will be fascinating and perhaps determinative.

No such dilemmas are to be found for Pat Murphy and the Brewers, at least insofar as their Game 5 starter is concerned. Jacob Misiorowski, the 24-year-old NL Cy Young favorite and the hardest-throwing starting pitcher anyone's ever seen, on Wednesday will make his fourth start of these playoffs. Last time out, Misiorowski in Game 1 against the Rays went five innings and permitted only one run en route to picking up the win. "Miz" also enjoyed a velocity bump compared to his prior run of starts.

However, he was coming off 11 days of rest in that start, and for his Game 5 trip to the bump he'll be on the standard four days of rest. He's well into career-high-workload territory in 2026, so it remains to be seen whether the sizzle he showed in the series opener will be back for Game 5. The Brewers could use some length from him given how hard the bullpen worked in Game 4.

The Rays' best hitter and one of the richest power sources in all of baseball had to exit Game 4 in the 12th inning not long after reaching base on Joey Ortiz's throwing error. He did so because of an injury to his left foot. From afar, this seems like the kind of knock that would earn Caminero a few days off had it occurred in, say, June, but this is very much not June.

"Junior, he's fine and obviously in the lineup today. Really impressive that he went first and third right there, very instinctual play," Cash said on Wednesday.

"He's been dealing with some lower extremity injuries, but there's a lot of guys that are nicked up right now playing through a lot and know that Cammy will be ready to go today."

The heart of the matter is whether Caminero will be in top form less than 24 hours after sustaining the injury. That's worth pondering in light of his ongoing power outage. Caminero this postseason has a respectable .717 OPS, but he has only one home run in 48 at-bats. That's after hitting a whopping 42 homers during the regular season and averaging one every 14.7 at-bats. It's quite possible that the Rays will need some customary thump from the hard-hitting 23-year-old if they're going to extend the series. That we shall see.

#2658. Rangers lose star goaltender Igor Shesterkin for season with lower-body injury; what's next for New York?

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

New York Rangers goaltender Igor Shesterkin will miss the remainder of the season with a lower-body injury, the team announced on Saturday.

Shesterkin suffered an apparent leg injury in the Rangers' loss to the Washington Capitals on Friday night as his right leg slid awkwardly into the post while scrambling to get back in position. Shesterkin fell to the ice immediately, and he needed assistance to get down the tunnel.

Prior to that loss, the Rangers were off to a terrific 4-1-0 start, and Shesterkin was a driving force behind that success. In just five appearances, Shesterkin posted 3.90 goals saved above average with a .900 high-danger save percentage, according to Natural Stat Trick.

The 2022 Vezina Trophy winner, Shesterkin has put up sparkling numbers since he entered the NHL in 2019-20. In 330 games, Shesterkin boasts a .917 save percentage, a 2.51 GAA and 22 shutouts. Over the last three full seasons from 2023-26, Shesterkin ranked third in goals saved above average with 45.4. Only Connor Hellebuyck and Andrei Vasilevskiy were better in that category.

Shesterkin was a big reason why the Rangers felt they could bounce back from a disappointing 2025-26 season, and losing the star goaltender puts a huge dent in the team's playoff hopes. It doesn't help that backup goalie Joonas Korpisalo is also hurt.

Dylan Garand replaced Shesterkin on Friday night, and Spencer Martin will be recalled from the AHL after recovering from his own injury. With the Rangers playing well early, it wouldn't be a shock to see them explore better replacement options for Shesterkin.

New York won't be able to replace Shesterkin's impact because he's one of the five best goalies in the world. However, the team should be able to upgrade its current goaltending situation, which is a fairly low bar to clear.

First, there are unsigned veterans still on the open market in Petr Mrazek and James Reimer. Neither one was great last season -- hence their availability at the moment -- Reimer and Mrazek could provide a level of stability in the crease that the Rangers simply don't have right now.

New York could also explore trade possibilities, and Minnesota Wild netminder Filip Gustavsson could be a solution there. Jesper Wallstedt is the future of the crease in Minnesota, making Gustavsson more of a luxury. Would the Wild send Gustavsson to New York in exchange for some draft capital it could use to acquire a center?

The one snag in a potential Gustavsson deal is his contract. Gustavsson is in the first year of a deal that pays him $6.8 million over the next five seasons. That's a big commitment for a player who will become a backup when Shesterkin returns.

Obviously, Connor Hellebuyck has been on the trade market for months now, but that trade wouldn't make sense for the Rangers. Hellebuyck is on an expensive long-term deal, and New York would have $20 million tied up in goalies if they made that move, not to mention the astronomical acquisition cost.

However, if you'll allow me to get creative here, it's no secret that the Florida Panthers have pursed Hellebuyck. What if the Panthers traded Jacob Markstrom -- just acquired in the offseason -- to the Rangers in order to make room for Hellebuyck?

Markstrom does have a 20-team no-trade list, so the question is whether New York would be one of his 11 approved teams. Florida flipping Markstrom so quickly seems like a long shot, but the team has taken plenty of big swings in recent history.

#2653. Ernie Johnson says he's stepping away from 'Inside the NBA' following the 2026-27 season

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Ernie Johnson announced on social media Wednesday that this will be his final season as the host of "Inside the NBA." The 2026-27 season is Johnson's 37th as the host of the popular pre- and post-game show featuring himself, Charles Barkley, Shaquille O'Neal and Kenny Smith, which has been a staple of NBA coverage since its debut in 1989.

"This will be my last season," Johnson said. "Totally my decision. It's just time. It's been an honor to share so many nights, decades actually, with my brothers."

Although Johnson, 70, is stepping away from his role on "Inside the NBA" after this season, he will still be part of TNT and CBS Sports' March Madness coverage, he announced in a nearly three-minute-long video.

It’s time.🤟🤟🏾🤟🏻🤟🏽 pic.twitter.com/h1qNwsnkUY

"Just to be clear, I'm not retiring," Johnson said. "Just cutting back. I'll still do March Madness and other projects for TNT and CBS, and I've just started a new production company called 32 Bowties geared toward telling feel-good stories in sports. So this is by no means the end. It's just a turning of the page. I'll forever cherish every chapter we have written with Inside the NBA."

Barkley, who is a staple on "Inside the NBA," said last month on an episode of "The Bill Simmons Podcast" that this season would also be his last unless Johnson changed his mind to return beyond this season.

"Me and Ernie are a package deal," Barkley said. "Ernie said to me, 'Chuck, would you please stay for two more years?' I said, 'I love you, man. You're the best. I'll stay for two more years.' So right now, unless Ernie changes his mind, next year is my last year, 100 percent. … If he says he's done, I'm gone."
